JavaScript

JavaScript · Section 1

Getting started

Study notes

What is JavaScript

The idea: JavaScript is the language that makes web pages do things. HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, and JavaScript gives behavior (clicks, forms, live updates). It was created in 1995 at Netscape, in about ten days, by Brendan Eich. Today it also runs on servers (Node.js), in mobile apps and in desktop apps.

Remember:

  • The official standard is called ECMAScript. Versions are named ES5, ES6/ES2015, ES2016... and a new one comes out every year.
  • It is dynamically typed: a variable can hold any type, and types are checked while the code runs.
  • It is single-threaded but non-blocking, thanks to the event loop.
  • An engine runs the code: V8 (Chrome, Node), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari).

Watch out: Java and JavaScript are unrelated languages. The similar name was a marketing choice.

Code editor

The idea: You can write JavaScript in any text editor, but a code editor helps with colors, auto-complete and error hints. Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is the most common choice.

Setup steps: install VS Code, open a folder, create index.html and app.js, and add extensions: ESLint (catches mistakes), Prettier (formats code) and Live Server (refreshes the browser on save). Install Node.js too, so you can run .js files from the terminal.

The browser console

The idea: Every browser has developer tools (press F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I, then open the Console tab). The console is a playground: type JavaScript, press Enter, and see the result at once. It also shows errors from your page, with the file and line number.

2 + 3            // 5 - the console prints the value right away
console.log('hi');      // normal message
console.warn('careful'); // yellow
console.error('broken'); // red, with stack trace
console.table([{a: 1}, {a: 2}]); // neat table
$0               // the element you selected in the Elements tab

Tip: Use the console to test small ideas before putting them in your project.

Hello World

The idea: The first program just prints a message, to prove your setup works. In a web page, JavaScript goes inside a <script> tag, either inline or as a separate file.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <body>
    <h1 id="title"></h1>
    <script src="app.js"></script>  <!-- put scripts at the end of body, or use defer -->
  </body>
</html>

// app.js
console.log('Hello, World!');
document.getElementById('title').textContent = 'Hello, World!';

Watch out: If the script runs before the HTML element exists, getElementById returns null. Place the script at the end of <body> or add defer.

Practice · 8 questions

Q1What is JavaScript, and where does it run?Show answer

JavaScript is a high-level, dynamically typed, single-threaded language. It runs in browsers (V8 in Chrome, SpiderMonkey in Firefox) and on servers through runtimes like Node.js, Deno and Bun.

// Same code, two places
console.log(typeof window !== 'undefined' ? 'Browser' : 'Node or other runtime');
Q2What is the difference between JavaScript and ECMAScript?Show answer

ECMAScript is the written standard (the rules). JavaScript is the most popular language built on that standard. ES6 (2015) means the 6th edition of the standard.

Q3Is JavaScript compiled or interpreted?Show answer

Both. Modern engines parse the code, start running it with an interpreter, then use a JIT (just-in-time) compiler to turn hot code into fast machine code.

Q4How do you add JavaScript to an HTML page? What do async and defer do?Show answer

Use a <script> tag. A plain script blocks HTML parsing. defer downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in order. async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it is ready, in any order.

<script src="app.js" defer></script>   <!-- safe for DOM code -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>  <!-- independent script -->
Q5What is the browser console used for?Show answer

To run quick code, see logs and errors, and inspect values. Useful methods beyond log:

console.table([{ id: 1, name: 'Asha' }, { id: 2, name: 'Ravi' }]);
console.error('Something failed');
console.time('loop'); for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++); console.timeEnd('loop');
Q6Why is JavaScript called single-threaded? Can it do two things at once?Show answer

It has one call stack, so it runs one piece of code at a time. It still handles many tasks by handing slow work (timers, network) to the runtime and picking up results later through the event loop (see Section 17).

Q7Which code editor would you use for JavaScript, and what extensions help?Show answer

Visual Studio Code is the most common choice. It is free and has a built-in terminal, debugger and Git support. Useful extensions: ESLint (finds bugs and bad patterns), Prettier (auto-formats code), and Live Server (reloads the page when you save).

Q8Show three ways to print "Hello, World!".Show answer
console.log('Hello, World!');               // 1. browser console or Node
document.body.textContent = 'Hello, World!'; // 2. on the web page
alert('Hello, World!');                      // 3. popup box (browser only)

To run it with Node, save it as hello.js and run node hello.js in the terminal.

JavaScript · Section 2

Fundamentals

Study notes

Syntax

The idea: Syntax is the grammar of the language. A program is a list of statements (instructions like let x = 5; or if (...) {}). Inside statements are expressions (pieces that produce a value, like x * 2).

Remember:

  • JavaScript is case-sensitive: name and Name are different.
  • Identifiers (names) may use letters, digits, _ and $, but cannot start with a digit or be a keyword (if, class, return...).
  • Spaces and new lines mostly do not matter, except after return.
  • Comments: // one line and /* many lines */.
  • Semicolons are optional, but use them to avoid surprises.

Variables

The idea: A variable is a named box that holds a value. Declare it with let (can change), const (cannot be reassigned) or the old var.

let count = 0;       // can change later
count = count + 1;
const PI = 3.14;     // fixed binding
let city;            // declared, value is undefined
let a = 1, b = 2;    // several at once

Watch out: Assigning to a name you never declared (total = 5) silently creates a global in non-strict code.

Data types

The idea: Every value has a type. There are 7 primitive types and 1 object type.

Type Example Notes
string 'hi' text
number 42, 3.5 integers and decimals share one type
bigint 10n very large integers
boolean true yes/no
undefined undefined not given a value
null null empty on purpose
symbol Symbol('id') unique key
object {}, [], functions everything else

Use typeof to check. Remember typeof null is 'object' (an old bug).

Number

The idea: All numbers (whole and decimal) are stored as 64-bit floating point. So decimals can have tiny rounding errors, and integers are exact only up to 2^53 − 1.

0.1 + 0.2;                 // 0.30000000000000004
(0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2);    // '0.30'
10 / 0;                    // Infinity
'abc' * 2;                 // NaN (not a number)
Number.isNaN(NaN);         // true
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;   // 9007199254740991

Tip: For money, store paise/cents as whole numbers to avoid decimal errors.

Numeric separator

The idea: You can put _ between digits so big numbers are easy to read. The value does not change.

const salary = 1_20_000;   // 120000 (Indian grouping works too)
const bytes  = 1_048_576;

Rule: _ must sit between two digits: not at the start, end, or next to a dot.

Octal and binary literals

The idea: You can write numbers in other bases with a prefix: 0b binary, 0o octal, 0x hex. They are still normal numbers.

0b101;   // 5
0o10;    // 8
0xff;    // 255
(255).toString(2); // '11111111' - convert back to a base
parseInt('ff', 16); // 255

Boolean

The idea: A boolean is true or false. In conditions, any value is turned into a boolean. Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.

Boolean('hello'); // true
Boolean(0);       // false
if ([]) {}        // runs - empty array is truthy

String

The idea: A string is text. Write it with 'single', "double" or backticks. Backticks (template literals) allow ${expressions} and multiple lines. Strings cannot be changed in place; methods return new strings.

const name = 'Ravi';
const msg = `Hello ${name}, you have ${2 + 3} messages`;
name.length;           // 4
name[0];               // 'R'
name.toUpperCase();    // 'RAVI'
'a' + 'b';             // 'ab'
'He said \"hi\"';      // escape quotes with backslash

Object

The idea: An object groups related data as key–value pairs (properties). Values can be anything, including functions (then they are called methods).

const user = { name: 'Asha', age: 25, greet() { return 'Hi ' + this.name; } };
user.name;            // dot notation
user['age'];          // bracket notation (needed for dynamic keys)
user.city = 'Hyd';    // add
delete user.age;      // remove
'name' in user;       // true

Primitive vs reference values

The idea: A primitive is copied when you assign it, so each variable has its own value. An object is shared: the variable holds a reference (an address), so two variables can point to the same object.

let a = 10; let b = a; b = 20;  // a stays 10
const o1 = { n: 1 }; const o2 = o1; o2.n = 2; // o1.n is now 2

Picture it: a primitive is a number written on paper; an object is a house, and the variable holds its address. Copying the address does not build a new house.

Array

The idea: An array is an ordered list. Indexes start at 0. Arrays are objects, so they are copied by reference.

const fruits = ['apple', 'mango'];
fruits.push('kiwi');        // add to end
fruits.unshift('grape');    // add to start
fruits.pop();               // remove from end
fruits.indexOf('mango');    // 2
fruits.includes('apple');   // true
fruits.length;              // 3
const copy = [...fruits];   // shallow copy

Watch out: typeof [] is 'object'. Use Array.isArray() to test for arrays.

Practice · 21 questions

Q1What are the data types in JavaScript?Show answer

Seven primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. Everything else is an object (arrays, functions, dates are objects too).

typeof 'hi';        // 'string'
typeof 42;          // 'number'
typeof 10n;         // 'bigint'
typeof Symbol();    // 'symbol'
typeof undefined;   // 'undefined'
typeof null;        // 'object'  <- famous old bug
typeof [];          // 'object'
typeof function(){} // 'function'
Q2Why does typeof null return 'object'? How do you check for null or arrays?Show answer

It is a bug from the first version of JavaScript that was never fixed, to avoid breaking old websites. Check null with === null and arrays with Array.isArray().

const v = null;
console.log(v === null);          // true
console.log(Array.isArray([1,2]));// true
Q3What is the difference between undefined and null?Show answer

undefined means a value was never given (the engine sets it). null means "empty on purpose" (the developer sets it).

let a;            // undefined
let b = null;     // empty on purpose
null == undefined;  // true  (loose)
null === undefined; // false (strict)
Q4Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3? How do you compare decimals safely?Show answer

Numbers are 64-bit floating point (IEEE 754). Some decimals cannot be stored exactly, so tiny errors appear. Compare with a small tolerance.

0.1 + 0.2;                                   // 0.30000000000000004
Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON;  // true
Q5What are NaN, Infinity, and Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER?Show answer

NaN is "not a number" from a failed math step, and it is not equal to itself. Infinity comes from dividing by zero. MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1) is the largest integer stored exactly; beyond it, use BigInt.

NaN === NaN;           // false
Number.isNaN(NaN);     // true  (prefer this over global isNaN)
isNaN('abc');          // true  (converts first - surprising)
Number.isNaN('abc');   // false
2 ** 53 === 2 ** 53 + 1; // true - precision lost
Q6What is the numeric separator?Show answer

Underscores inside number literals to make them easier to read. They do not change the value.

const budget = 1_000_000;
const bytes = 0b1111_0000;
console.log(budget); // 1000000
Q7How do you write binary, octal and hex numbers?Show answer
0b1010; // 10  binary
0o17;   // 15  octal (old style 017 is an error in strict mode)
0xff;   // 255 hex
Q8What are truthy and falsy values?Show answer

Falsy values become false in a condition. There are only eight: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including '0', [] and {}.

if ([]) console.log('empty array is truthy');
if ('0') console.log("'0' is truthy");
Boolean('');  // false
Q9Strings are immutable. What does that mean?Show answer

You cannot change a character inside a string. Methods return a new string.

let s = 'cat';
s[0] = 'b';         // ignored
console.log(s);     // 'cat'
s = 'b' + s.slice(1);
console.log(s);     // 'bat'
Q10Primitive vs reference values: what is the difference?Show answer

Primitives are copied by value. Objects are copied by reference, so two variables can point to the same object.

let x = 5; let y = x; y = 10;
console.log(x); // 5

const p1 = { name: 'Asha' };
const p2 = p1;
p2.name = 'Ravi';
console.log(p1.name); // 'Ravi' - same object
Q11How do you copy an object or array? Shallow vs deep copy?Show answer

Spread and Object.assign make shallow copies (nested objects are still shared). structuredClone makes a deep copy.

const user = { name: 'A', address: { city: 'Hyd' } };
const shallow = { ...user };
shallow.address.city = 'Pune';
console.log(user.address.city); // 'Pune' - shared!

const deep = structuredClone(user);
deep.address.city = 'Delhi';
console.log(user.address.city); // 'Pune' - safe
Q12How do you compare two objects for equality?Show answer

=== checks if both point to the same object, not if contents match. For contents, compare keys yourself or use a library.

({ a: 1 }) === ({ a: 1 }); // false
const o = { a: 1 };
o === o;                    // true
JSON.stringify({a:1}) === JSON.stringify({a:1}); // true (key order matters)
Q13Common array tasks: add, remove, find. Which methods change the array?Show answer

push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse change (mutate) the array. map, filter, slice, concat, toSorted, toReversed return a new one.

const nums = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = nums.toSorted();  // [1,2,3], nums unchanged
nums.sort();                     // nums is now [1,2,3]
nums.splice(1, 1);               // removes 1 item at index 1 -> [1,3]
Q14Why does [10, 1, 2].sort() give [1, 10, 2]?Show answer

Default sort compares items as strings. Pass a compare function for numbers.

[10, 1, 2].sort();               // [1, 10, 2]
[10, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10]
Q15What is the difference between length and the last index, and what happens if you set length?Show answer
const arr = [1, 2, 3, 4];
arr.length = 2;
console.log(arr);   // [1, 2]  - extra items removed
console.log(arr.at(-1)); // 2 - at() supports negative index
Q16What is the difference between a statement and an expression?Show answer

An expression produces a value (2 + 3, x > 5, fn()). A statement performs an action (if, for, let x = 1;). You can use an expression wherever a value is expected, but not a statement.

const grade = score > 50 ? 'Pass' : 'Fail'; // ternary is an expression - works
// const g = if (score > 50) { 'Pass' };    // SyntaxError - if is a statement
Q17What are the rules for naming identifiers? Is JavaScript case-sensitive?Show answer

A name can contain letters, digits, _ and $, but cannot start with a digit. It cannot be a reserved keyword (class, return, let, ...). JavaScript is case-sensitive, so total and Total are different variables.

let userName = 'a', _private = 1, $el = null; // valid
// let 2fast = 1;   // SyntaxError: starts with a digit
// let class = 1;   // SyntaxError: reserved word
let total = 1, Total = 2; // two different variables
Q18Are semicolons required? What can go wrong without them?Show answer

Usually not, because of Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI). But a line that starts with ( or [ can join with the line above it and cause a bug.

const a = 1
const b = a
[1, 2].forEach(n => console.log(n))
// read as: const b = a[1, 2].forEach(...)  -> TypeError

Safe habit: always use semicolons, or let a tool like Prettier add them.

Q19How do you write comments?Show answer
// single-line comment
/* multi-line
   comment */
/**
 * JSDoc comment - editors show this as a hint
 * @param {number} r radius
 */
function area(r) { return Math.PI * r * r; }
Q20What happens if you assign to a variable you never declared?Show answer

In normal (sloppy) mode it silently creates a global variable, which causes hidden bugs. In strict mode it throws a ReferenceError. Modules and classes are always strict.

function sloppy() { leaked = 5; }
sloppy();
console.log(leaked); // 5 - accidental global

'use strict';
function strict() { oops = 5; } // ReferenceError when called
Q21Undefined vs undeclared: how do you safely check?Show answer

An undefined variable exists but has no value. An undeclared variable was never created; reading it throws an error. typeof is safe for both.

let x;
x === undefined;        // true
// y === undefined;     // ReferenceError: y is not defined
typeof y === 'undefined'; // true - no error

JavaScript · Section 3

Operators

Study notes

Arithmetic operators

The idea: + - * / % ** do math. The tricky one is +: with any string on either side, it joins text instead of adding. The other operators always convert to numbers.

7 / 2;      // 3.5 - no integer division
Math.floor(7 / 2); // 3
'7' + 1;    // '71'
'7' - 1;    // 6
'7' * '2';  // 14

Watch out: Values from forms and prompt() are always strings. Convert with Number() before adding.

Remainder operator

The idea: a % b gives what is left after dividing a by b. The result takes the sign of a.

10 % 3;   // 1
-10 % 3;  // -1

Common uses: check even/odd (n % 2 === 0), wrap around a list ((i + 1) % length), every Nth item (i % 5 === 0).

Assignment operators

The idea: = stores a value. Compound forms combine a math step with storing: x += 2 means x = x + 2.

Operator Same as
x += y x = x + y
x -= y x = x - y
x *= y x = x * y
x /= y x = x / y
x %= y x = x % y
x **= y x = x ** y

An assignment is also an expression that returns the stored value, so a = b = 5 sets both.

Unary operators

The idea: Unary operators work on one value.

  • +x turns x into a number; -x turns it into a number and flips the sign.
  • ++x / x++ add 1; --x / x-- subtract 1. Prefix returns the new value, postfix returns the old one.
  • !x gives the opposite boolean; typeof x gives the type name; delete obj.key removes a property.
let n = 1;
const a = n++;  // a = 1, n = 2
const b = ++n;  // b = 3, n = 3
+'3.5';         // 3.5

Comparison operators

The idea: < > <= >= == != === !== compare two values and return a boolean.

Remember:

  • === and !== compare without type conversion. Use them by default.
  • == converts types first, so '1' == 1 is true. The only common good use is x == null, which checks for both null and undefined.
  • Strings compare letter by letter by character code: 'apple' < 'b' is true, '10' < '9' is true.
  • NaN is not equal to anything, even itself.
  • Objects compare by reference: {} === {} is false.

Logical operators

The idea: ! (NOT), && (AND), || (OR). && and || stop early (short-circuit) and return one of the actual values, not always a boolean.

true && 'yes';    // 'yes' - all truthy, returns last
0 && 'yes';       // 0     - stops at first falsy
null || 'guest';  // 'guest' - returns first truthy
isLoggedIn && showDashboard();   // run only if true
const port = config.port || 3000; // default value

Order of priority: ! first, then &&, then ||. Use brackets when mixing them.

Watch out: || replaces valid values like 0 and ''. Use ?? for defaults (see Section 19).

Practice · 11 questions

Q1What does + do with a string and a number? What about -?Show answer

If either side of + is a string, it joins strings. Other math operators (-, *, /) convert both sides to numbers.

'5' + 2;   // '52'
'5' - 2;   // 3
'5' * '2'; // 10
1 + 2 + '3'; // '33'  (left to right: 3 + '3')
'1' + 2 + 3; // '123'
Q2What is the difference between == and ===?Show answer

=== (strict) compares type and value with no conversion. == (loose) converts types first, which gives surprising results. Use === by default.

0 == '';          // true
0 == '0';         // true
'' == '0';        // false  - not transitive!
null == undefined;// true
null == 0;        // false
0 === '';         // false
Q3What does Object.is() do differently from ===?Show answer

It fixes two edge cases: NaN equals NaN, and +0 is not equal to -0.

NaN === NaN;          // false
Object.is(NaN, NaN);  // true
0 === -0;             // true
Object.is(0, -0);     // false
Q4What is the remainder operator, and how is it different from modulo with negatives?Show answer

% returns the remainder and keeps the sign of the left number. True modulo always returns a positive value for a positive divisor.

7 % 3;   // 1
-7 % 3;  // -1
const mod = (n, d) => ((n % d) + d) % d;
mod(-7, 3); // 2
const isEven = n => n % 2 === 0;
Q5Prefix vs postfix increment: what is the difference?Show answer

++x adds first, then returns the new value. x++ returns the old value, then adds.

let a = 5;
console.log(a++); // 5, a is now 6
console.log(++a); // 7
Q6What does the unary + do?Show answer

It converts a value to a number. Quick, but Number() is easier to read.

+'42';   // 42
+'';     // 0
+'abc';  // NaN
+true;   // 1
+[];     // 0
+{};     // NaN
Q7What do && and || actually return?Show answer

They return one of the operands, not always true/false. || returns the first truthy value; && returns the first falsy value (or the last value if all are truthy). This is called short-circuit evaluation.

'' || 'default';      // 'default'
'Asha' || 'default';  // 'Asha'
0 && 'never';         // 0
'a' && 'b';           // 'b'
user && user.name;    // safe access (older style)
Q8Why is !! used?Show answer

Double NOT converts any value to its boolean form.

!!'text'; // true
!!0;      // false
!!null;   // false
Q9How does comparing strings work?Show answer

Strings compare character by character using Unicode code values, so uppercase letters come before lowercase. Use localeCompare for human sorting.

'apple' < 'banana'; // true
'Z' < 'a';          // true (code 90 < 97)
'10' < '9';         // true (string compare)
10 < 9;             // false
['b','a','C'].sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y)); // ['a','b','C']
Q10What are compound assignment operators?Show answer
let total = 10;
total += 5;  // 15
total *= 2;  // 30
total **= 2; // 900
total %= 7;  // 4
Q11Tricky output questionsShow answer
[] + [];       // ''
[] + {};       // '[object Object]'
true + true;   // 2
'3' - - '3';   // 6
[] == ![];     // true  ([] -> '' -> 0, ![] -> false -> 0)

Explain these by naming the steps: each side is converted to a primitive, then to a number or string.

JavaScript · Section 4

Control flow

Study notes

if, if...else, if...else if

The idea: Run code only when a condition is truthy. else gives a fallback. else if adds more checks, tested from top to bottom; only the first true branch runs.

const temp = 32;
if (temp > 35) {
  console.log('Very hot');
} else if (temp > 25) {
  console.log('Warm');      // this runs
} else {
  console.log('Cool');
}

Remember: always use {} even for one line. It prevents bugs when you add a second line later. Put the most specific condition first.

Ternary operator

The idea: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse is a short if...else that returns a value, so you can use it inside an assignment or template string.

const fee = age < 12 ? 50 : 100;
console.log(`You are ${isMember ? 'a member' : 'a guest'}`);

Watch out: nested ternaries quickly become unreadable. Switch to if when there are more than two outcomes.

switch

The idea: Compare one value against many exact cases using ===. Each case usually ends with break; without it, execution "falls through" into the next case. default runs when nothing matches.

switch (role) {
  case 'admin':
    access = 'full';
    break;
  case 'editor':
  case 'author':          // two cases share one block
    access = 'write';
    break;
  default:
    access = 'read';
}

Tip: switch (true) { case score >= 90: ... } lets you use ranges, but an if chain is usually clearer.

while

The idea: Repeat while a condition stays true. The condition is checked before each round, so the body might never run. Use it when you don't know how many rounds you need.

let balance = 1000, months = 0;
while (balance < 2000) {
  balance *= 1.05;   // 5% growth
  months++;
}

Watch out: if nothing inside the loop changes the condition, you get an infinite loop that freezes the page.

do...while

The idea: Like while, but the condition is checked after each round, so the body always runs at least once. Good for "ask until the answer is valid".

let guess;
do {
  guess = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10);
} while (guess !== 7);

for loop

The idea: for (start; condition; step) puts the counter setup, check and update on one line. Best when you know the number of rounds.

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) console.log(i);        // 0..4
for (let i = 10; i > 0; i -= 2) console.log(i);    // 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
const arr = ['a', 'b'];
for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) console.log(i, arr[i]);

All three parts are optional: for (;;) {} is an infinite loop.

break and continue

The idea: break exits the loop (or switch) completely. continue skips the rest of this round and goes to the next. Labels let break exit an outer loop.

for (const n of [3, -1, 8, 0, 5]) {
  if (n < 0) continue;  // skip negatives
  if (n === 0) break;   // stop at zero
  console.log(n);       // 3, 8
}

Comma operator

The idea: a, b evaluates both and returns b. Its main real use is updating two loop variables at once.

const word = 'level';
let isPal = true;
for (let i = 0, j = word.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--) {
  if (word[i] !== word[j]) { isPal = false; break; }
}

Note: the commas in let a = 1, b = 2 and in function arguments are separators, not the comma operator.

Practice · 12 questions

Q1When would you use switch instead of if...else if?Show answer

When you compare one value against many fixed options. switch uses strict equality (===). Forgetting break causes fall-through into the next case.

function dayType(day) {
  switch (day) {
    case 'Sat':
    case 'Sun':
      return 'Weekend';   // grouped cases on purpose
    case 'Mon':
      console.log('Start of week');
      // no break -> falls through!
    default:
      return 'Weekday';
  }
}
dayType('Mon'); // logs 'Start of week', returns 'Weekday'
Q2How can you replace a long switch with an object lookup?Show answer
const prices = { tea: 20, coffee: 40, juice: 60 };
const getPrice = item => prices[item] ?? 'Not on menu';
getPrice('coffee'); // 40
Q3When should you use the ternary operator, and when not?Show answer

Use it for a simple choice between two values. Avoid nesting many ternaries; it hurts reading.

const age = 20;
const label = age >= 18 ? 'Adult' : 'Minor';
Q4while vs do...while: what is the difference?Show answer

while checks the condition first (may run zero times). do...while runs the body once before checking (runs at least once).

let n = 10;
while (n < 5) { console.log('never'); }
do { console.log('runs once'); } while (n < 5);
Q5What is the output? (classic var in a loop question)Show answer
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// 3 3 3  - one shared i, callbacks run after the loop ends

for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);
}
// 0 1 2  - let makes a new j for each loop round
Q6break vs continue?Show answer

break exits the loop fully. continue skips the rest of the current round and moves to the next.

for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  if (i === 2) continue; // skip 2
  if (i === 4) break;    // stop at 4
  console.log(i);        // 1, 3
}
Q7How do you break out of nested loops?Show answer

Use a label.

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
    if (i * j === 2) break outer;
    console.log(i, j);
  }
}
Q8Can you break out of forEach?Show answer

No. forEach always visits every item. Use for...of, some, every or find if you need to stop early.

[1, 2, 3, 4].some(n => {
  console.log(n);
  return n === 2;  // returning true stops the loop
}); // logs 1, 2
Q9What is the comma operator?Show answer

It runs expressions left to right and returns the last one. Mostly seen in for loops to update two variables.

for (let i = 0, j = 5; i < j; i++, j--) {
  console.log(i, j); // 0 5, 1 4, 2 3
}
const x = (1, 2, 3); // 3
Q10Write FizzBuzz (a common warm-up).Show answer
for (let i = 1; i <= 15; i++) {
  let out = '';
  if (i % 3 === 0) out += 'Fizz';
  if (i % 5 === 0) out += 'Buzz';
  console.log(out || i);
}
Q11In an if...else if chain, why does the order of conditions matter?Show answer

Conditions are checked top to bottom, and only the first true branch runs. Put the most specific check first, or broader checks will catch values too early.

function grade(score) {
  if (score >= 50) return 'Pass';        // wrong order: 95 stops here
  else if (score >= 90) return 'Distinction';
}
function gradeFixed(score) {
  if (score >= 90) return 'Distinction'; // most specific first
  else if (score >= 50) return 'Pass';
  else return 'Fail';
}
Q12What is a guard clause (early return), and why is it preferred over deep nesting?Show answer
// Nested
function checkout(cart, user) {
  if (user) {
    if (cart.length > 0) {
      return 'Order placed';
    }
  }
}
// Guard clauses: handle bad cases first, keep the main path flat
function checkoutClean(cart, user) {
  if (!user) return 'Please log in';
  if (cart.length === 0) return 'Cart is empty';
  return 'Order placed';
}

JavaScript · Section 5

Functions

Study notes

Functions

The idea: A function is a reusable block of code with a name. You give it inputs (parameters), it does work, and it can give back an output with return. Write once, call many times.

function calcGST(price, rate = 18) {   // declaration
  return price * rate / 100;
}
calcGST(1000);      // 180
calcGST(1000, 5);   // 50

Remember:

  • Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass in.
  • Missing arguments become undefined; extra arguments are ignored (but available in arguments / rest).
  • Without return, a function returns undefined. return also stops the function at once.
  • Function declarations are hoisted (callable before the line); function expressions are not.

Functions are first-class citizens

The idea: In JavaScript a function is a value, just like a number. So you can store it in a variable, put it in an array or object, pass it to another function, and return it from a function. This is what makes callbacks, map/filter and closures possible.

const ops = {
  add: (a, b) => a + b,
  mul: (a, b) => a * b
};
function calculate(op, a, b) { return ops[op](a, b); }
calculate('mul', 3, 4);  // 12

function greeter(greeting) {          // returns a function
  return name => `${greeting}, ${name}`;
}
const namaste = greeter('Namaste');
namaste('Ravi');                       // 'Namaste, Ravi'

Anonymous functions

The idea: A function without a name. You usually create it on the spot, to pass as an argument or to store in a variable.

setTimeout(function () { console.log('done'); }, 1000);
[1, 2, 3].map(function (n) { return n * 10; });
[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 10);  // arrow version, also anonymous

Watch out: anonymous functions show up as "anonymous" in error stack traces, and they cannot call themselves by name. Name them when debugging matters.

Pass-by-value

The idea: When you call a function, JavaScript copies each argument into the parameter. For a primitive, the copy is the value, so the caller's variable never changes. For an object, the copy is the reference, so the function can change the object's insides but cannot swap the caller's variable to a new object.

function tryChange(num, obj) {
  num = 99;            // only local copy changes
  obj.status = 'paid'; // same object -> caller sees it
  obj = {};            // local variable now points elsewhere
}
let n = 1; const order = { status: 'new' };
tryChange(n, order);
n;             // 1
order.status;  // 'paid'

Tip: to avoid surprising callers, return a new object instead of changing the one passed in: return { ...obj, status: 'paid' }.

Recursive functions

The idea: A function that calls itself to solve a smaller piece of the same problem. Every recursive function needs (1) a base case that stops, and (2) a recursive step that moves toward the base case.

function countdown(n) {
  if (n < 0) return;      // base case
  console.log(n);
  countdown(n - 1);       // smaller problem
}

function fib(n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }

// Good fit: tree-shaped data
function totalSize(folder) {
  return folder.files.reduce((s, f) => s + f.size, 0)
       + folder.subfolders.reduce((s, sub) => s + totalSize(sub), 0);
}

Watch out: no base case means infinite calls and a "Maximum call stack size exceeded" error. Plain fib is also very slow for big n; add memoization.

Default parameters

The idea: Give a parameter a fallback value right in the definition. It is used when the argument is missing or exactly undefined.

function createUser(name, role = 'viewer', createdAt = new Date()) {
  return { name, role, createdAt };
}
createUser('Asha');              // role 'viewer'
createUser('Asha', undefined);   // role 'viewer'
createUser('Asha', null);        // role null - null is a real value

Remember: default expressions run at call time (a fresh new Date() each call), and they can use earlier parameters: function f(a, b = a * 2).

Practice · 10 questions

Q1Function declaration vs function expression: what is the difference?Show answer

A declaration is hoisted whole, so you can call it before the line where it is written. An expression is stored in a variable and only exists after that line runs.

sayHi();                 // works
function sayHi() { console.log('Hi'); }

sayBye();                // TypeError (var) or ReferenceError (let/const)
const sayBye = function () { console.log('Bye'); };
Q2What does "functions are first-class citizens" mean?Show answer

Functions are values. You can store them in variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions.

const double = n => n * 2;
const apply = (fn, value) => fn(value);      // passed in
const multiplier = k => n => n * k;           // returned
apply(double, 5);        // 10
const triple = multiplier(3);
triple(4);               // 12
Q3What is a higher-order function? Give examples.Show answer

A function that takes a function as input or returns one. map, filter, reduce and setTimeout are common examples.

const prices = [100, 250, 80];
const withTax = prices.map(p => p * 1.18);
const cheap = prices.filter(p => p < 200);
const total = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0); // 430
Q4What is an anonymous function, and what is the downside?Show answer

A function with no name, often used as a callback. Downside: stack traces are harder to read. Named function expressions help.

setTimeout(function () { console.log('anon'); }, 0);
const factorial = function fact(n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); };
Q5Is JavaScript pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?Show answer

Always pass-by-value. For objects, the value passed is a reference (an address). So you can change the object's properties, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

function update(obj) {
  obj.score = 100;        // changes caller's object
  obj = { score: 0 };     // only changes local variable
}
const player = { score: 10 };
update(player);
console.log(player.score); // 100
Q6What is recursion? What is the risk?Show answer

A function that calls itself, with a base case to stop. Risk: too many calls cause "Maximum call stack size exceeded".

function sumTo(n) {
  if (n === 0) return 0;      // base case
  return n + sumTo(n - 1);    // recursive case
}
sumTo(5); // 15

// Flatten a nested array
const flat = arr => arr.reduce(
  (acc, x) => acc.concat(Array.isArray(x) ? flat(x) : x), []);
flat([1, [2, [3, [4]]]]); // [1, 2, 3, 4]
Q7How do default parameters work? When is the default used?Show answer

The default is used only when the argument is undefined (missing or passed as undefined), not for null. Defaults can use earlier parameters.

function greet(name = 'Guest', msg = `Hello ${name}`) {
  return msg;
}
greet();           // 'Hello Guest'
greet(undefined);  // 'Hello Guest'
greet(null);       // 'Hello null'
Q8What is the arguments object?Show answer

An array-like object with all passed arguments, available in regular functions (not arrow functions). Today, rest parameters (...args) are preferred.

function show() {
  console.log(arguments.length, Array.from(arguments));
}
show(1, 2, 3); // 3 [1, 2, 3]
Q9What does a function return if there is no return?Show answer
function noReturn() {}
console.log(noReturn()); // undefined

function tricky() {
  return      // automatic semicolon inserted here!
  { ok: true };
}
console.log(tricky());   // undefined
Q10What is a pure function?Show answer

Same input always gives the same output, and it has no side effects (does not change outside data). Pure functions are easy to test.

const add = (a, b) => a + b;                 // pure
let count = 0;
const addToCount = n => (count += n);        // impure: changes outside state

JavaScript · Section 6

Objects & prototypes

Study notes

Object methods

The idea: A method is a function stored as a property. Inside it, this refers to the object the method was called on, so the method can read and change that object's data.

const cart = {
  items: [],
  add(item) { this.items.push(item); return this; }, // return this -> chaining
  count() { return this.items.length; }
};
cart.add('pen').add('book').count(); // 2

Constructor functions

The idea: A normal function, called with new, that builds objects of one shape. By habit its name starts with a capital letter.

function Product(name, price) {
  this.name = name;
  this.price = price;
}
const p = new Product('Pen', 20);  // { name: 'Pen', price: 20 }

Watch out: forgetting new runs it as a plain function, so this is undefined (strict mode) and you get an error or global leak.

Prototype

The idea: Every object has a hidden link, [[Prototype]], to another object. When you read a property that the object doesn't have, JavaScript follows that link and looks there, then the next link, until it reaches null. This is the prototype chain. Functions have a prototype property; objects made with new Fn() link to Fn.prototype.

const arr = [1, 2];
arr.map;   // found on Array.prototype, not on arr itself
Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype;            // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype; // true

Picture it: a chain arr → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null.

Constructor/prototype pattern

The idea: Put data that differs per object inside the constructor (this.x = ...). Put shared methods on Fn.prototype, so all objects reuse one copy.

function Product(name, price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; }
Product.prototype.withTax = function () { return this.price * 1.18; };
new Product('Pen', 100).withTax(); // 118

ES6 classes do exactly this behind the scenes.

Prototypal inheritance

The idea: Objects inherit straight from other objects. Object.create(proto) makes a new object whose prototype is proto. The child can add or override properties; anything missing is looked up on the parent.

const vehicle = { wheels: 4, describe() { return `${this.wheels} wheels`; } };
const bike = Object.create(vehicle);
bike.wheels = 2;            // overrides (shadows) parent's value
bike.describe();            // '2 wheels' - method from parent, this = bike

this

The idea: this is decided by how a function is called:

Call style this is
obj.method() obj
fn() undefined (strict) / global object
new Fn() the new object
fn.call(x), apply, bind x
arrow function this of the surrounding code
DOM event handler (regular function) the element

Watch out: pulling a method out of its object (const f = obj.method) or passing it as a callback loses this. Fix with bind or an arrow function.

globalThis

The idea: One name for the global object that works everywhere: browser (window), Node (global), web worker (self). Use it in code meant to run in many environments.

globalThis.appVersion = '1.0';
console.log(globalThis.appVersion);

Object properties

The idea: Each property is either a data property (holds a value) or an accessor property (has get/set functions). Each one also has flags: writable (can change), enumerable (shows up in loops) and configurable (can be deleted or redefined). Normal properties have all flags true.

const acc = { _bal: 0, get balance() { return `Rs ${this._bal}`; } };
acc.balance; // 'Rs 0' - getter runs
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(acc, '_bal');
// { value: 0, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }

for...in loop

The idea: Loops over the keys of an object, including inherited enumerable keys. Use Object.hasOwn to skip inherited ones. Prefer Object.keys/entries for plain objects and for...of for arrays.

const marks = { maths: 90, science: 85 };
for (const subject in marks) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(marks, subject)) console.log(subject, marks[subject]);
}

Enumerable properties

The idea: "Enumerable" means "shows up when you list the keys". Properties you create normally are enumerable. Built-in methods and properties made with defineProperty (default) are not, so they stay out of for...in, Object.keys, spread and JSON.stringify, but you can still read them directly. Check with obj.propertyIsEnumerable('key').

Own properties

The idea: An own property lives directly on the object. An inherited property comes from the prototype chain. in checks both; Object.hasOwn (or hasOwnProperty) checks own only.

const parent = { a: 1 };
const child = Object.create(parent); child.b = 2;
'a' in child;              // true
Object.hasOwn(child, 'a'); // false
Object.keys(child);        // ['b'] - own + enumerable only

Factory functions

The idea: A plain function that creates and returns an object. No new, no this confusion, and local variables stay private through closure.

function createWallet(owner) {
  let balance = 0;                     // private
  return {
    owner,
    deposit(x) { balance += x; },
    getBalance: () => balance
  };
}
const w = createWallet('Asha'); w.deposit(100); w.getBalance(); // 100
w.balance;  // undefined - cannot touch it

Trade-off: each object gets its own copy of the methods (uses more memory than prototypes for thousands of objects).

Object destructuring

The idea: Pull properties out of an object into variables in one line. You can rename, set defaults, go into nested objects and collect the rest.

const order = { id: 42, total: 999, customer: { name: 'Ravi' } };
const { id, total: amount, status = 'pending', customer: { name } } = order;
// id=42, amount=999, status='pending', name='Ravi'

function printOrder({ id, total }) { console.log(id, total); } // in parameters

Watch out: destructuring null or undefined throws. Give a default: function f({ a } = {}).

Optional chaining (?.)

The idea: a?.b returns undefined instead of crashing when a is null or undefined. Works for properties (?.), brackets (?.[ ]) and calls (?.()).

const user = { profile: null };
user.profile?.email;            // undefined (no TypeError)
user.settings?.['theme'];       // undefined
user.onLogin?.();               // called only if onLogin is not null/undefined
const email = user.profile?.email ?? 'not set';

Watch out: don't sprinkle ?. everywhere; it can hide real bugs where a value should always exist.

Object literal syntax extensions

The idea: ES6 shortcuts for writing objects: shorthand properties ({ name } instead of { name: name }), shorthand methods (greet() {}), and computed keys ([expression]: value).

const field = 'email', value = 'a@b.com';
const form = {
  field,
  [field + 'Valid']: true,  // emailValid: true
  submit() { return 'sent'; }
};

Practice · 16 questions

Q1What are the ways to create an object?Show answer
const a = { x: 1 };                       // object literal
const b = new Object();                   // Object constructor
const c = Object.create(protoObj);        // with a chosen prototype
function Car(m) { this.model = m; }
const d = new Car('Swift');               // constructor function
class Bike { constructor(m) { this.model = m; } }
const e = new Bike('Pulsar');             // class
Q2What happens when you call a function with new?Show answer

Four steps: (1) a new empty object is made, (2) its prototype is set to Fn.prototype, (3) the function runs with this pointing to the new object, (4) the new object is returned (unless the function returns another object).

function myNew(Fn, ...args) {
  const obj = Object.create(Fn.prototype);
  const result = Fn.apply(obj, args);
  return result instanceof Object ? result : obj;
}
Q3What is a prototype and the prototype chain?Show answer

Every object has a hidden link to another object called its prototype. When a property is not found on the object, JavaScript looks up this chain until it reaches null.

const animal = { eats: true };
const dog = Object.create(animal);
dog.barks = true;
dog.eats;                              // true (from prototype)
Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal; // true
dog.hasOwnProperty('eats');            // false
Q4Why put methods on the prototype instead of inside the constructor?Show answer

Methods on the prototype are shared by all instances (one copy in memory). Methods inside the constructor are copied for every object.

function User(name) { this.name = name; }
User.prototype.greet = function () { return `Hi ${this.name}`; };
const u1 = new User('A'), u2 = new User('B');
u1.greet === u2.greet; // true - shared
Q5How did inheritance work before classes?Show answer
function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; };

function Dog(name) { Animal.call(this, name); }      // borrow constructor
Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype);     // link prototypes
Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog;

new Dog('Tommy').speak(); // 'Tommy makes a sound'
Q6How is the value of this decided?Most askedShow answer

It depends on how a function is called, not where it is written. Four rules, in order of priority:

  1. new Fn() → this is the new object.
  2. fn.call(obj) / apply / bind → this is obj.
  3. obj.fn() → this is obj.
  4. Plain fn() → undefined in strict mode, the global object otherwise.

Arrow functions ignore these rules; they take this from the surrounding code.

const person = {
  name: 'Asha',
  hi() { return this.name; },
  later() { setTimeout(() => console.log(this.name), 0); } // arrow keeps this
};
person.hi();            // 'Asha'
const hi = person.hi;
hi();                   // undefined - lost the object
person.later();         // 'Asha'
Q7What is globalThis?Show answer

A standard name for the global object in any environment: window in browsers, global in Node, self in workers.

Q8What are property descriptors? How do you make a read-only property?Show answer

Each property has hidden flags: writable, enumerable, configurable (or get/set).

const cfg = {};
Object.defineProperty(cfg, 'apiUrl', {
  value: 'https://api.example.com',
  writable: false, enumerable: true, configurable: false
});
cfg.apiUrl = 'x';   // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(cfg, 'apiUrl');
Q9Object.freeze vs Object.seal vs Object.preventExtensions?Show answer
Method Add new props Delete props Change values
preventExtensions No Yes Yes
seal No No Yes
freeze No No No

All three are shallow; nested objects can still change.

Q10for...in vs Object.keys vs for...of?Show answer

for...in loops over enumerable keys, including inherited ones. Object.keys gives only own enumerable keys. for...of loops over values of iterables (arrays, strings, maps), not plain objects.

const base = { inherited: 1 };
const obj = Object.create(base);
obj.own = 2;
for (const k in obj) console.log(k);  // own, inherited
Object.keys(obj);                     // ['own']
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) console.log(k, v); // own 2
Q11How do you check if a property exists?Show answer
const o = { a: undefined };
'a' in o;                  // true (own or inherited)
Object.hasOwn(o, 'a');     // true (own only, modern)
o.a !== undefined;         // false - misleading!
Q12What is a factory function, and how is it different from a constructor?Show answer

A plain function that returns a new object. No new, no this problems, and it can keep private data with closures.

function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;                          // private
  return { inc: () => ++count, get: () => count };
}
const c = createCounter();
c.inc(); c.get(); // 1
Q13Object destructuring: rename, default and nested values.Show answer
const user = { id: 7, profile: { city: 'Hyd' } };
const { id: userId, role = 'guest', profile: { city } } = user;
console.log(userId, role, city); // 7 'guest' 'Hyd'

const { id, ...rest } = user;     // rest = { profile: {...} }
Q14What does optional chaining ?. do?Show answer

It stops and returns undefined if the value before it is null or undefined, instead of throwing an error.

const order = { customer: null };
order.customer?.address?.city;   // undefined, no error
order.getTotal?.();              // call only if the method exists
const first = order.items?.[0];  // safe index
Q15What are object literal shorthand features?Show answer
const name = 'Asha', key = 'role';
const obj = {
  name,                 // shorthand property
  [key]: 'admin',       // computed key
  greet() { return 'hi'; } // shorthand method
};
Q16What is an enumerable property? Which tools skip non-enumerable ones?Show answer

A property is enumerable when its enumerable flag is true. Properties you add normally are enumerable. Built-in methods (like toString) and properties made with Object.defineProperty (default false) are not. for...in, Object.keys, Object.entries, spread and JSON.stringify skip non-enumerable properties.

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.defineProperty(user, 'id', { value: 7 }); // enumerable: false by default
Object.keys(user);                    // ['name']
JSON.stringify(user);                 // '{"name":"Asha"}'
user.id;                              // 7 - still readable
user.propertyIsEnumerable('id');      // false
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(user);     // ['name', 'id'] - includes hidden ones

↑ Back to contents

JavaScript · Section 7

Classes

Study notes

Class

The idea: A class is a blueprint for objects, with a cleaner syntax than constructor functions. The constructor runs on new; other methods go on the prototype automatically.

class Student {
  constructor(name, marks) {
    this.name = name;
    this.marks = marks;
  }
  average() {
    return this.marks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / this.marks.length;
  }
}
const s = new Student('Asha', [80, 90]);
s.average(); // 85

Remember: class code always runs in strict mode; a class must be called with new; class declarations are not usable before their line (TDZ); methods are not enumerable.

Getters and setters

The idea: get and set make a method look like a normal property. A getter computes a value when read; a setter runs checks when written.

class Rectangle {
  constructor(w, h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
  get area() { return this.w * this.h; }      // r.area, no ()
  set width(v) {
    if (v <= 0) throw new Error('Width must be positive');
    this.w = v;
  }
}
const r = new Rectangle(2, 3);
r.area;       // 6
r.width = 5;  // setter runs

Watch out: a getter with no setter makes the property read-only. Assigning to it is ignored (or throws in strict mode).

Class expressions

The idea: Like function expressions, a class can be created inside an expression and stored in a variable, passed to a function, or returned. This enables "mixins" (functions that add features to a class).

const Serializable = Base => class extends Base {
  toJSON() { return JSON.stringify(this); }
};
class User { constructor(n) { this.n = n; } }
const SUser = Serializable(User);
new SUser('a').toJSON(); // '{"n":"a"}'

Computed properties

The idea: Put an expression in [ ] to make a method or property name at runtime. Most common use: [Symbol.iterator] to make a class iterable.

const prefix = 'get';
class Api {
  [`${prefix}Users`]() { return ['a', 'b']; }
}
new Api().getUsers();

Inheritance (extends, super)

The idea: class Child extends Parent makes Child reuse Parent's methods. In the child constructor, call super(...) first to run the parent constructor. Override a method by defining it again; call the parent version with super.method().

class Employee {
  constructor(name, salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; }
  pay() { return this.salary; }
}
class Manager extends Employee {
  constructor(name, salary, bonus) {
    super(name, salary);   // must be before using this
    this.bonus = bonus;
  }
  pay() { return super.pay() + this.bonus; } // override + reuse
}
new Manager('Ravi', 50000, 10000).pay(); // 60000

Remember: you can also extend built-ins: class MyError extends Error {}.

new.target

The idea: Inside a function or constructor, new.target tells you which class was called with new (or undefined if called without new). Use it to make abstract base classes, or to force new.

function Person(name) {
  if (!new.target) return new Person(name); // works with or without new
  this.name = name;
}

Static methods

The idea: A static method belongs to the class, not to objects made from it. Call it as ClassName.method(). Use it for helpers and factory methods that don't need one specific object.

class Temperature {
  static cToF(c) { return c * 9 / 5 + 32; }
  static fromF(f) { return new Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9); }
  constructor(c) { this.c = c; }
}
Temperature.cToF(100); // 212

Inside a static method, this is the class itself.

Static properties

The idea: A static field is one value shared by the class (like a class-level counter or config), not copied into each object.

class Order {
  static count = 0;
  static TAX = 0.18;
  constructor() { this.id = ++Order.count; }
}
new Order(); new Order();
Order.count; // 2

Private fields

The idea: A field whose name starts with # can only be read or written inside the class body. Outside code gets a SyntaxError. This protects internal data from accidental changes.

class Counter {
  #value = 0;
  increment() { this.#value++; }
  get value() { return this.#value; }
}
const c = new Counter(); c.increment();
c.value;   // 1
// c.#value  -> SyntaxError

Remember: private fields must be declared at the top of the class; they are not visible in Object.keys or JSON.stringify.

Private methods

The idea: Methods named with # are helpers that only the class itself can call. They keep the public API small.

class Signup {
  #isValidEmail(e) { return /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$/.test(e); }
  register(email) {
    if (!this.#isValidEmail(email)) throw new Error('Bad email');
    return 'registered';
  }
}

There are also private static methods and private getters/setters, written the same way with #.

Practice · 10 questions

Q1Are JavaScript classes real classes like in Java?Show answer

No. A class is mostly cleaner syntax over constructor functions and prototypes. Under the hood, typeof MyClass is 'function'. Differences from plain functions: classes are not hoisted for use, always run in strict mode, and must be called with new.

class Point {
  constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
  toString() { return `(${this.x}, ${this.y})`; }
}
typeof Point;               // 'function'
Point.prototype.toString;   // method lives on the prototype
Point();                    // TypeError: needs 'new'
Q2How do getters and setters work? Why use them?Show answer

They let you run code when a property is read or written, for example to validate input or compute a value.

class Temperature {
  #celsius = 0;
  get fahrenheit() { return this.#celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }
  set celsius(v) {
    if (v < -273.15) throw new RangeError('Below absolute zero');
    this.#celsius = v;
  }
}
const t = new Temperature();
t.celsius = 100;
t.fahrenheit; // 212
Q3What is a class expression?Show answer

A class defined inside an expression, like a function expression. Useful for creating classes on the fly.

const Shape = class { area() { return 0; } };
const withLogging = Base => class extends Base {
  log() { console.log('area:', this.area()); }
};
new (withLogging(Shape))().log(); // area: 0  (a "mixin")
Q4What are computed property names in classes?Show answer
const method = 'sayHi';
class Bot {
  [method]() { return 'hi'; }
  [Symbol.iterator]() { return [1, 2].values(); }
}
new Bot().sayHi(); // 'hi'
[...new Bot()];    // [1, 2]
Q5How do extends and super work?Show answer

extends sets up the prototype chain. In a child constructor you must call super() before using this. super.method() calls the parent's version.

class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name, breed) {
    super(name);           // must come first
    this.breed = breed;
  }
  speak() { return super.speak() + ' (woof)'; }
}
new Dog('Tommy', 'Lab').speak(); // 'Tommy makes a sound (woof)'
Q6What does instanceof check?Show answer

Whether Class.prototype appears anywhere in the object's prototype chain.

const d = new Dog('T', 'X');
d instanceof Dog;    // true
d instanceof Animal; // true
d instanceof Object; // true
Q7What is new.target? Build an abstract class with it.Show answer

Inside a constructor, new.target points to the class that was called with new. You can use it to block direct creation of a base class.

class Shape {
  constructor() {
    if (new.target === Shape) throw new TypeError('Shape is abstract');
  }
}
class Circle extends Shape {}
new Circle(); // ok
new Shape();  // TypeError
Q8Static methods and static properties: what are they for?Show answer

They belong to the class itself, not to instances. Good for helpers, factories and shared counters.

class User {
  static count = 0;
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; User.count++; }
  static fromJSON(json) { return new User(JSON.parse(json).name); }
}
const u = User.fromJSON('{"name":"Asha"}');
User.count;   // 1
u.fromJSON;   // undefined - not on instances
Q9How do private fields and methods work?Show answer

Names starting with # can only be used inside the class body. This is real privacy, enforced by the language (not just a naming habit like _name).

class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0;
  #log(msg) { console.log(`[bank] ${msg}`); }
  deposit(amt) {
    if (amt <= 0) throw new Error('Invalid amount');
    this.#balance += amt;
    this.#log(`deposited ${amt}`);
  }
  get balance() { return this.#balance; }
  static isAccount(obj) { return #balance in obj; } // brand check
}
const acc = new BankAccount();
acc.deposit(500);
acc.balance;   // 500
acc.#balance;  // SyntaxError
Q10Why can a class method lose this when used as a callback? How do you fix it?Show answer
class Clicker {
  count = 0;
  handle() { this.count++; }
  handleArrow = () => { this.count++; };  // class field arrow: this is fixed
}
const c = new Clicker();
const h = c.handle;
// h();                 // TypeError: this is undefined
const bound = c.handle.bind(c); bound();  // fix 1: bind
const f = c.handleArrow; f();             // fix 2: arrow field

JavaScript · Section 8

Advanced functions

Study notes

Function type

The idea: Every function is an object of type Function. So it has properties (name, length) and methods (call, apply, bind, toString). You can even attach your own properties to it.

function greet(first, last) {}
greet.name;      // 'greet'
greet.length;    // 2 (declared parameters)
typeof greet;    // 'function'
greet instanceof Object; // true

call()

The idea: fn.call(thisValue, arg1, arg2) runs the function now, with this set to thisValue and arguments listed one by one. Use it to borrow a method from another object.

function describe(city) { return `${this.name} lives in ${city}`; }
describe.call({ name: 'Asha' }, 'Hyderabad'); // 'Asha lives in Hyderabad'

// borrowing: use an array method on an array-like object
const args = { 0: 'a', 1: 'b', length: 2 };
Array.prototype.join.call(args, '-'); // 'a-b'

apply()

The idea: Same as call, but the arguments come as one array. Handy when your arguments are already in an array (though spread ... now covers most of these cases).

describe.apply({ name: 'Ravi' }, ['Pune']);
Math.max.apply(null, [3, 9, 4]); // 9  (modern: Math.max(...arr))

bind()

The idea: fn.bind(thisValue, ...args) does not run the function. It returns a new function with this locked forever (and optionally some arguments pre-filled). Use it for callbacks and event handlers that would otherwise lose this.

const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  tick() { this.seconds++; }
};
setInterval(timer.tick.bind(timer), 1000); // this stays timer

const double = ((a, b) => a * b).bind(null, 2); // partial application
double(7); // 14

Remember: a bound function cannot be re-bound; the first bind wins.

Closures

The idea: When a function is created inside another function, it keeps a live link to the outer function's variables, even after the outer function has returned. That remembered environment is the closure. Each call of the outer function creates a fresh set of variables.

function makeRateLimiter(limit) {
  let used = 0;                       // kept alive by the closure
  return function () {
    if (used >= limit) return 'Limit reached';
    used++;
    return `Request ${used} ok`;
  };
}
const apiCall = makeRateLimiter(2);
apiCall(); apiCall(); apiCall(); // 'Request 1 ok', 'Request 2 ok', 'Limit reached'

Where you see closures: private variables, counters, function factories, memoize, debounce/throttle, event handlers, setTimeout callbacks, React hooks.

Watch out: closures keep variables in memory; a closure holding a big object can cause a memory leak if the function lives forever.

IIFE

The idea: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression is a function that is defined and run in one step: (function () { ... })();. Variables inside it stay private. It was the main way to avoid global variables before let/const and modules.

const config = (() => {
  const env = 'prod';              // private
  return { apiUrl: env === 'prod' ? 'https://api.site.com' : 'http://localhost' };
})();

(async () => {                      // still useful: run await at top level in old scripts
  const data = await fetch('/api').then(r => r.json());
})();

Watch out: if the line before an IIFE has no semicolon, the ( joins with it. That is why you sometimes see ;(function(){})().

Returning multiple values

The idea: A function returns only one value, so wrap several values in an array (when order is clear) or an object (when names help), then destructure at the call site.

function divide(a, b) { return [Math.floor(a / b), a % b]; }
const [quotient, remainder] = divide(17, 5); // 3, 2

function getBounds(nums) { return { min: Math.min(...nums), max: Math.max(...nums) }; }
const { max } = getBounds([4, 8, 1]); // 8 - pick just what you need

Arrow functions

The idea: A short way to write functions: (params) => expression. With one expression and no braces, the value is returned automatically. Arrows have no own this, arguments, super or prototype, and cannot be used with new.

const square = x => x * x;               // one param: no () needed
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const log = () => console.log('hi');      // no params: empty ()
const toObj = id => ({ id });             // return an object: wrap in ()
const process = items => {                // braces: need return
  const valid = items.filter(Boolean);
  return valid.length;
};

When not to use arrow functions

The idea: Because arrows take this from outside, they are wrong where you need a dynamic this:

  • Object methods that use this (it won't be the object).
  • Prototype methods and class getters that need the instance (use normal methods).
  • Constructors (arrows can't be called with new).
  • DOM event handlers that use this to mean the clicked element.
  • Functions that need arguments (use rest params instead).
button.addEventListener('click', function () {
  this.classList.toggle('active');   // this = button
});

Rest parameters

The idea: ...name as the last parameter gathers all remaining arguments into a real array. It replaces the old arguments object.

function logAll(level, ...messages) {
  messages.forEach(m => console.log(`[${level}] ${m}`));
}
logAll('INFO', 'started', 'connected');

Rules: only one rest parameter, and it must be last. Rest does not count toward fn.length.

Callbacks

The idea: A callback is a function you hand to another function, so that function can call it later: after each item (map), after an event (click), or after slow work finishes (a timer or network request).

// synchronous callback
[3, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b);

// asynchronous callback (Node style: error first)
function loadUser(id, done) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (id <= 0) done(new Error('Invalid id'));
    else done(null, { id, name: 'Asha' });
  }, 500);
}
loadUser(1, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return console.error(err.message);
  console.log(user.name);
});

Watch out: many nested async callbacks become "callback hell": hard to read and to handle errors in. Promises (Section 9) solve this.

Practice · 14 questions

Q1Functions are objects. What properties do they have?Show answer

name (the function's name), length (number of declared parameters before any default or rest), and prototype (for regular functions).

function add(a, b, c = 0) {}
add.name;    // 'add'
add.length;  // 2 - stops at the default
add.calls = 0; // you can attach your own properties
Q2call vs apply vs bind?Most askedShow answer

All three set this. call runs now with arguments one by one. apply runs now with arguments as an array. bind does not run; it returns a new function with this (and optional arguments) locked in.

function intro(greeting, punct) { return `${greeting}, I am ${this.name}${punct}`; }
const asha = { name: 'Asha' };

intro.call(asha, 'Hi', '!');      // 'Hi, I am Asha!'
intro.apply(asha, ['Hello', '.']); // 'Hello, I am Asha.'
const later = intro.bind(asha, 'Hey');
later('?');                        // 'Hey, I am Asha?'

Memory trick: Apply = Array, Call = Comma.

Q3Write your own bind (polyfill).Show answer
Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...preset) {
  const fn = this;
  return function (...later) {
    return fn.apply(ctx, [...preset, ...later]);
  };
};
Q4What is a closure?Most askedShow answer

A closure is a function plus the variables it remembers from where it was created. The inner function keeps access to outer variables even after the outer function has finished.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;               // remembered by the inner function
  return function () { return ++count; };
}
const c1 = makeCounter();
c1(); c1();        // 2
const c2 = makeCounter();
c2();              // 1 - its own separate count

Uses: private data, function factories, memoization, debounce/throttle, event handlers.

Q5Use a closure to memoize (cache) a slow function.Show answer
function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return function (n) {
    if (cache.has(n)) return cache.get(n);
    const result = fn(n);
    cache.set(n, result);
    return result;
  };
}
const slowSquare = n => { for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++); return n * n; };
const fastSquare = memoize(slowSquare);
fastSquare(9); // slow first time
fastSquare(9); // instant
Q6Write a debounce function.Show answer

Debounce waits until calls stop for a set time, then runs once. Useful for search boxes.

function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timer;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay);
  };
}
const search = debounce(q => console.log('searching', q), 300);
search('j'); search('ja'); search('jav'); // only 'jav' runs
Q7Write a throttle function.Show answer

Throttle runs at most once per time window. Useful for scroll and resize.

function throttle(fn, wait) {
  let last = 0;
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= wait) { last = now; fn.apply(this, args); }
  };
}
Q8What is an IIFE and why was it used?Show answer

An Immediately Invoked Function Expression runs as soon as it is defined. Before modules and let, it was used to create a private scope and avoid polluting globals.

const counterModule = (function () {
  let count = 0;
  return { inc: () => ++count };
})();
counterModule.inc(); // 1
Q9How do you return multiple values from a function?Show answer
function minMax(arr) {
  return [Math.min(...arr), Math.max(...arr)];   // array
}
const [lo, hi] = minMax([4, 9, 1]);

function stats(arr) {
  const sum = arr.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return { sum, avg: sum / arr.length };          // object (order-free)
}
const { avg } = stats([2, 4, 6]); // 4
Q10How are arrow functions different from regular functions?Show answer
Feature Regular function Arrow function
Own this Yes (depends on call) No (taken from outer scope)
arguments object Yes No
Can use new Yes No
Has prototype Yes No
Implicit return No Yes, for one expression 
const sq = x => x * x;
const makeObj = () => ({ ok: true }); // wrap object in () to return it
Q11When should you NOT use arrow functions?Show answer

As object methods that need this, as prototype methods, as constructors, and as DOM event handlers where you need this to be the element.

const counter = {
  count: 0,
  incBad: () => this.count++,   // this is NOT counter
  incGood() { this.count++; }
};
Q12Rest parameters vs spread syntax?Show answer

Same ... look, opposite jobs. Rest collects many values into one array (in parameters). Spread expands an array or object into separate values (in calls and literals).

const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // rest
sum(1, 2, 3);                  // 6
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
Math.max(...arr);              // spread -> 3
const merged = { ...{ a: 1 }, b: 2 };
Q13What is a callback? What is "callback hell"?Show answer

A callback is a function passed to another function, to be called later. Callback hell is deep nesting of async callbacks, which is hard to read and handle errors in. Promises and async/await fix this.

getUser(1, user => {
  getOrders(user.id, orders => {
    getDetails(orders[0], details => {
      console.log(details);   // pyramid of doom
    });
  });
});
Q14What is currying?Show answer

Turning a function with many arguments into a chain of functions that each take one.

const curry = fn => function curried(...args) {
  return args.length >= fn.length
    ? fn.apply(this, args)
    : (...more) => curried.apply(this, [...args, ...more]);
};
const add3 = curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c);
add3(1)(2)(3); // 6
add3(1, 2)(3); // 6
