JavaScript · Section 9

Promises & async/await

Study notes

Promises

The idea: A promise is a receipt for a result that isn't ready yet, like an order token at a food counter. It starts pending, then becomes fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). It settles only once. You attach handlers with .then() for success and .catch() for failure.

function orderFood(item) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      item === 'dosa' ? resolve('Dosa ready') : reject(new Error('Out of stock'));
    }, 1000);
  });
}
orderFood('dosa')
  .then(msg => console.log(msg))
  .catch(err => console.log(err.message));

Remember: .then callbacks always run asynchronously, even for an already-resolved promise. Promise.resolve(x) and Promise.reject(err) create settled promises quickly.

Promise chaining

The idea: .then() returns a new promise, so you can line up steps. A step's return value is passed to the next step; if it returns a promise, the chain waits for it. One .catch() at the end handles an error from any step.

login('asha', 'pw')
  .then(user => getCart(user.id))      // return the promise!
  .then(cart => calculateTotal(cart))
  .then(total => console.log('Pay', total))
  .catch(err => console.error('Failed at some step:', err));

Watch out: forgetting return inside .then means the next step gets undefined and doesn't wait.

Promise.all()

The idea: Run many promises at the same time and wait for all of them. You get an array of results in the same order as the input. If any one rejects, the whole thing rejects at once.

const [user, posts, friends] = await Promise.all([
  fetchUser(1), fetchPosts(1), fetchFriends(1)
]);

Use when: every result is required (loading a dashboard).

Promise.race()

The idea: Settles as soon as the first promise settles, whether it succeeds or fails. Others keep running but are ignored.

Use when: adding a timeout, or taking whichever mirror server answers first.

Promise.any()

The idea: Resolves with the first promise that succeeds, ignoring failures. Rejects only if all fail, with an AggregateError holding every error.

const fastest = await Promise.any([
  fetch('https://cdn1.example.com/lib.js'),
  fetch('https://cdn2.example.com/lib.js')
]);

Promise.allSettled()

The idea: Waits for all promises to finish, never rejects, and reports each outcome as { status: 'fulfilled', value } or { status: 'rejected', reason }.

const results = await Promise.allSettled(emails.map(sendEmail));
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === 'rejected').length;
console.log(`${failed} emails failed`);

Use when: you want every result even if some fail (bulk jobs, reports).

Promise finally()

The idea: .finally(fn) runs fn after the promise settles, success or failure. It receives no value and passes the original result or error through unchanged. Perfect for cleanup.

setLoading(true);
saveForm(data)
  .then(() => toast('Saved'))
  .catch(() => toast('Error'))
  .finally(() => setLoading(false));  // always runs

Promise error handling

The idea: Inside a promise chain, a thrown error or a rejected promise skips the remaining .then steps and jumps to the next .catch. After .catch handles it, the chain continues normally.

Remember:

  • Always end a chain with .catch(); otherwise you get an "unhandled rejection".
  • .then(onSuccess, onError)'s second argument does not catch errors thrown in onSuccess; a separate .catch does.
  • To pass an error further up, re-throw it inside .catch.
  • An error inside a setTimeout callback within the executor is NOT caught by the promise; call reject instead.

async / await

The idea: async before a function makes it always return a promise. Inside it, await promise pauses that function until the promise settles, then gives you the value (or throws the error). It reads like normal step-by-step code. Use try/catch for errors.

async function checkout(userId) {
  try {
    const cart = await getCart(userId);
    const total = await calculateTotal(cart);
    return `Paid ${total}`;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
    throw err;   // let caller know
  } finally {
    console.log('checkout attempt finished');
  }
}

Watch out: await one-after-another makes independent calls slow; start them together with Promise.all. And await inside forEach does not wait; use for...of.

Promise.withResolvers()

The idea: A new helper (ES2024) that returns { promise, resolve, reject }. It lets you create a promise now and resolve it later from somewhere else, without nesting your code inside new Promise(...).

function waitForEvent(el, type) {
  const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
  el.addEventListener(type, resolve, { once: true });
  return promise;
}
await waitForEvent(button, 'click');

Practice · 14 questions

Q1What is a Promise? What are its states?Show answer

A Promise is an object for a value that will be ready later. It has three states: pending, fulfilled (resolved with a value) or rejected (failed with a reason). Once settled, it never changes again.

const wait = ms => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  if (ms < 0) reject(new Error('Negative time'));
  setTimeout(() => resolve(`waited ${ms}ms`), ms);
});
wait(500).then(msg => console.log(msg)).catch(err => console.error(err));
Q2How does promise chaining work?Show answer

Each .then() returns a new promise. Whatever you return inside .then() becomes the input to the next one. If you return a promise, the chain waits for it.

fetch('/api/user/1')
  .then(res => res.json())          // returns a promise
  .then(user => fetch(`/api/orders/${user.id}`))
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(orders => console.log(orders.length))
  .catch(err => console.error('Any step failed:', err));

Common mistake: forgetting to return inside .then(), which breaks the chain.

Q3Compare Promise.all, allSettled, race and any.Most askedShow answer
Method Resolves when Rejects when
Promise.all All fulfill (array of values) Any one rejects (fail fast)
Promise.allSettled All settle (array of {status, value/reason}) Never
Promise.race First one settles (value) First one settles with an error
Promise.any First one fulfills All reject (AggregateError) 
const p1 = Promise.resolve(1);
const p2 = Promise.reject(new Error('x'));
const p3 = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(3), 100));

await Promise.all([p1, p3]);          // [1, 3]
await Promise.allSettled([p1, p2]);   // [{status:'fulfilled',value:1},{status:'rejected',reason:Error}]
await Promise.any([p2, p3]);          // 3
await Promise.race([p1, p3]);         // 1
Q4Use Promise.race to add a timeout to a request.Show answer
function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timed out')), ms));
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
}
withTimeout(fetch('/slow'), 2000).catch(e => console.log(e.message));
Q5What does .finally() do?Show answer

It runs after the promise settles, whether it passed or failed. It gets no value and does not change the result. Good for cleanup, like hiding a loader.

showLoader();
fetchData().then(render).catch(showError).finally(hideLoader);
Q6How do you handle errors in promises? What if you forget?Show answer

Use .catch() at the end of a chain, or try/catch with await. A throw inside .then() becomes a rejection. If no one catches it, you get an "unhandled promise rejection" (in Node this can crash the process).

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => { throw new Error('boom'); })
  .then(() => console.log('skipped'))
  .catch(e => console.log('caught:', e.message)) // caught: boom
  .then(() => console.log('chain continues'));
Q7What is async/await? How does it relate to promises?Show answer

It is cleaner syntax on top of promises. An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that function (not the whole program) until the promise settles.

async function loadUser(id) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Load failed', err);
    return null;
  }
}
loadUser(1).then(u => console.log(u)); // async fn returns a promise
Q8Sequential vs parallel awaits: what is the difference?Most askedShow answer
// Slow: second request waits for the first (~2s total)
const a = await getA(); // 1s
const b = await getB(); // 1s

// Fast: both start together (~1s total)
const [x, y] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);
Q9Why does await inside forEach not work as expected?Show answer

forEach ignores the promises returned by the callback, so it does not wait. Use for...of for one-by-one, or Promise.all with map for all-at-once.

const ids = [1, 2, 3];
// Wrong: logs 'done' before items finish
ids.forEach(async id => await save(id));
console.log('done');

// Right (sequential)
for (const id of ids) await save(id);
// Right (parallel)
await Promise.all(ids.map(id => save(id)));
Q10Predict the output order.Show answer
console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
(async () => { console.log('4'); await null; console.log('5'); })();
console.log('6');
// 1 4 6 3 5 2

A: Sync code runs first (1, 4, 6). Then all microtasks (promise callbacks: 3, 5). Then the next macrotask (timer: 2). See Section 17.

Q11What is Promise.withResolvers()?Show answer

A newer helper that returns { promise, resolve, reject } together, so you can resolve the promise from outside its constructor.

const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
button.addEventListener('click', () => resolve('clicked'), { once: true });
await promise; // waits for the click
Q12Convert a callback API into a promise (promisify).Show answer
function promisify(fn) {
  return (...args) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    fn(...args, (err, result) => err ? reject(err) : resolve(result));
  });
}
// const readFileP = promisify(fs.readFile);
Q13Implement Promise.all yourself.Show answer
function myAll(promises) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const results = [];
    let done = 0;
    if (promises.length === 0) return resolve([]);
    promises.forEach((p, i) => {
      Promise.resolve(p).then(value => {
        results[i] = value;              // keep order
        if (++done === promises.length) resolve(results);
      }, reject);
    });
  });
}
Q14Write a retry helper with delay.Show answer
async function retry(fn, tries = 3, delay = 500) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= tries; attempt++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (err) {
      if (attempt === tries) throw err;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, delay * attempt)); // back off
    }
  }
}

JavaScript · Section 10

Iterators & generators

Study notes

Iterators

The idea: Iteration is a shared agreement (a "protocol") so any loop can walk through any collection. Two parts:

  • Iterable: has a [Symbol.iterator]() method that hands out an iterator.
  • Iterator: has next(), which returns { value, done } each time it is called.

Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets and arguments are iterable. Plain objects are not. Anything iterable works with for...of, spread [...x], Array.from, destructuring and Promise.all.

const steps = {
  list: ['wake', 'brush', 'code'],
  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    let i = 0;
    return { next: () => ({ value: this.list[i], done: i++ >= this.list.length }) };
  }
};
[...steps]; // ['wake', 'brush', 'code']

Generators

The idea: A generator (function*) is a function that can pause. Each yield hands out a value and freezes the function; the next next() call resumes it right there. Calling the function only creates the generator object; nothing runs until next().

function* trafficLight() {
  while (true) {
    yield 'green';
    yield 'yellow';
    yield 'red';
  }
}
const light = trafficLight();
light.next().value; // 'green'
light.next().value; // 'yellow'

Why it's useful: writing iterators becomes easy, and values are produced lazily (only when asked), so infinite sequences are safe.

yield

The idea: yield value sends a value out and pauses. yield is also an expression: whatever you pass into the next next(x) comes back as its result. yield* iterable hands over to another iterable and yields all its values. A return inside a generator ends it with done: true.

function* runningTotal() {
  let total = 0;
  while (true) total += yield total;   // receive a number, send total
}
const t = runningTotal();
t.next();      // start: { value: 0 }
t.next(10);    // { value: 10 }
t.next(5);     // { value: 15 }

for...of

The idea: The simplest way to loop over the values of any iterable. It supports break, continue and await (as for await), unlike forEach.

for (const ch of 'hi') console.log(ch);                 // h, i
for (const [key, val] of new Map([['a', 1]])) console.log(key, val);
for (const [i, item] of ['x', 'y'].entries()) console.log(i, item);
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries({ a: 1 })) console.log(k, v); // plain objects

Watch out: for...of on a plain object throws "is not iterable". Use Object.entries first.

Async iterators

The idea: Same idea as iterators, but next() returns a promise of { value, done }. The object uses [Symbol.asyncIterator]. Loop with for await...of, which waits for each value before moving on. Good for data that arrives over time: paged APIs, file streams, websocket messages.

// Node: read a big file line by line without loading it all
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';
import { createInterface } from 'node:readline';
const lines = createInterface({ input: createReadStream('big.log') });
for await (const line of lines) {
  if (line.includes('ERROR')) console.log(line);
}

Async generators

The idea: async function* combines both: you can await inside and yield values out. The result is an async iterator, used with for await...of. It is the easiest way to build your own async stream.

async function* pollStatus(jobId) {
  while (true) {
    const res = await fetch(`/jobs/${jobId}`).then(r => r.json());
    yield res.status;
    if (res.status === 'done') return;
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000)); // wait 2s
  }
}
for await (const status of pollStatus(7)) console.log(status);

Practice · 11 questions

Q1What are the iterable and iterator protocols?Show answer

An iterable is an object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method. That method returns an iterator: an object with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Arrays, strings, Maps and Sets are built-in iterables.

const it = ['a', 'b'][Symbol.iterator]();
it.next(); // { value: 'a', done: false }
it.next(); // { value: 'b', done: false }
it.next(); // { value: undefined, done: true }
Q2Make a custom object iterable.Show answer
class Range {
  constructor(start, end) { this.start = start; this.end = end; }
  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    let current = this.start;
    const end = this.end;
    return {
      next: () => current <= end
        ? { value: current++, done: false }
        : { value: undefined, done: true }
    };
  }
}
for (const n of new Range(1, 3)) console.log(n); // 1 2 3
[...new Range(1, 4)];                            // [1, 2, 3, 4]
Q3What is a generator function?Show answer

A function written with function* that can pause at each yield and continue later. Calling it does not run the body; it returns a generator object (which is both an iterator and an iterable).

function* idMaker() {
  let id = 1;
  while (true) yield id++;   // infinite, but lazy - safe
}
const ids = idMaker();
ids.next().value; // 1
ids.next().value; // 2
Q4Rewrite the Range class with a generator.Show answer
class Range {
  constructor(s, e) { this.s = s; this.e = e; }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { for (let i = this.s; i <= this.e; i++) yield i; }
}
Q5How can you send values into a generator with next()?Show answer

The value passed to next(x) becomes the result of the paused yield expression. The first next() only starts the generator.

function* conversation() {
  const name = yield 'What is your name?';
  const city = yield `Hi ${name}, where do you live?`;
  return `${name} lives in ${city}`;
}
const g = conversation();
g.next().value;            // 'What is your name?'
g.next('Asha').value;      // 'Hi Asha, where do you live?'
g.next('Hyderabad').value; // 'Asha lives in Hyderabad'
Q6What does yield* do?Show answer

It hands control to another iterable or generator and yields all its values.

function* inner() { yield 2; yield 3; }
function* outer() { yield 1; yield* inner(); yield 4; }
[...outer()]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]

function* flatten(arr) {
  for (const x of arr) Array.isArray(x) ? yield* flatten(x) : yield x;
}
[...flatten([1, [2, [3]]])]; // [1, 2, 3]
Q7What do return() and throw() do on a generator?Show answer
function* g() {
  try { yield 1; yield 2; }
  finally { console.log('cleanup'); }
}
const it = g();
it.next();       // { value: 1, done: false }
it.return('x');  // logs 'cleanup', { value: 'x', done: true }

A break inside for...of also calls return(), so cleanup code runs.

Q8for...of vs for...in?Show answer

for...of gives values of an iterable. for...in gives keys (property names, as strings) of any object. Do not use for...in on arrays.

const arr = ['x', 'y'];
for (const v of arr) console.log(v); // 'x', 'y'
for (const k in arr) console.log(k); // '0', '1'
for (const [i, v] of arr.entries()) console.log(i, v); // 0 'x', 1 'y'
Q9Why are generators useful? Give real uses.Show answer

Lazy sequences (compute only what you need), infinite streams, custom iteration, and paging through API results.

function* take(iter, n) {
  for (const x of iter) { if (n-- <= 0) return; yield x; }
}
function* naturals() { let n = 1; while (true) yield n++; }
[...take(naturals(), 5)]; // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Q10What are async iterators and for await...of?Show answer

An async iterator's next() returns a promise. for await...of waits for each one in turn. Good for streams and paginated APIs.

async function* fetchPages(url) {
  let next = url;
  while (next) {
    const res = await fetch(next);
    const data = await res.json();
    yield data.items;
    next = data.nextPage;     // null when done
  }
}
for await (const items of fetchPages('/api/products?page=1')) {
  console.log('got', items.length);
}
Q11What is an async generator?Show answer

A function written with async function*. It can both await and yield, and it produces an async iterator.

async function* ticker(times, ms) {
  for (let i = 1; i <= times; i++) {
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
    yield i;
  }
}
for await (const t of ticker(3, 1000)) console.log('tick', t);

JavaScript · Section 11

Modules

Study notes

Modules

The idea: A module is one file with its own private scope. It shares only what it exports, and uses other files only through import. This splits a big app into small, focused files with clear dependencies.

Remember:

  • In the browser: <script type="module">. In Node: .mjs files or "type": "module" in package.json.
  • Modules are always strict mode and are deferred by default in browsers.
  • Each module runs once; every import shares the same instance.
  • Top-level this is undefined.

export

The idea: Mark what other files can use. Named exports (many per file, imported by exact name) or one default export (the file's main thing).

// cart.js
export const TAX = 0.18;                    // named
export function total(items) { /* ... */ }  // named
const helper = () => {};
export { helper as calc };                    // rename while exporting
export default class Cart {}                 // default

Tip: many teams prefer named exports: names stay consistent and editors can auto-import them.

import

The idea: Bring exports into the current file. Named imports go in { } and must match the name (rename with as); the default import takes any name you choose.

import Cart, { TAX, total as cartTotal } from './cart.js';
import * as cart from './cart.js';   // all exports as one object
import './polyfills.js';             // run a file for its side effects only

Remember: static import lines are hoisted and must be at the top level (not inside if or functions). Imported bindings are live and read-only.

Dynamic import()

The idea: import('./file.js') loads a module when the code runs and returns a promise. Use it to load heavy features only when needed (smaller first page load), or to pick a module based on a condition.

async function openEditor() {
  const { Editor } = await import('./editor.js');
  new Editor().mount('#app');
}

Top-level await

The idea: In a module, you can use await directly at the top of the file, outside any async function. Modules that import it wait until it finishes.

// db.js
export const db = await connectToDatabase();

Watch out: a slow top-level await blocks every module that depends on it. Works only in modules, not classic scripts or CommonJS.

Practice · 9 questions

Q1What is an ES module, and why use modules?Show answer

A module is a file with its own scope. Nothing leaks to the global scope unless exported. Modules give reuse, clear dependencies and better tree-shaking (removing unused code at build time). Modules always run in strict mode.

<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>  <!-- deferred by default -->
Q2Named exports vs default export?Show answer

A file can have many named exports but only one default export. Named imports must match the name (or be renamed with as). A default import can use any name.

// math.js
export const PI = 3.14159;
export function area(r) { return PI * r * r; }
export default function circumference(r) { return 2 * PI * r; }

// main.js
import circ, { PI, area as circleArea } from './math.js';
import * as math from './math.js';   // namespace import
math.area(2);
Q3What is re-exporting?Show answer

Exporting things from another module, often used in an index.js "barrel" file to give one import path.

// utils/index.js
export { formatDate } from './date.js';
export * from './string.js';
export { default as logger } from './logger.js';
Q4Are imports live bindings or copies?Show answer

Live, read-only bindings. If the exporting module changes the value, importers see the new value. Importers cannot reassign it.

// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export const inc = () => count++;

// main.js
import { count, inc } from './counter.js';
inc();
console.log(count); // 1 - live
// count = 5;       // TypeError: assignment to constant
Q5ES modules vs CommonJS (Node's require)?Show answer
Feature ES modules CommonJS
Syntax import / export require / module.exports
Loading Static, analyzed before run Dynamic, at run time
Bindings Live Copied value
Top-level await Yes No
this at top level undefined module.exports
Q6What is dynamic import()?Show answer

A function-like call that loads a module at run time and returns a promise. Used for code-splitting and loading features only when needed.

button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const { renderChart } = await import('./chart.js'); // loaded on demand
  renderChart(data);
});

const lang = navigator.language.startsWith('te') ? 'te' : 'en';
const messages = (await import(`./i18n/${lang}.js`)).default;
Q7What is top-level await? Any downside?Show answer

In ES modules you can use await outside an async function. Downside: any module that imports it must wait, so a slow await can delay app start.

// config.js
const res = await fetch('/config.json');
export const config = await res.json();

// main.js - waits until config.js is ready
import { config } from './config.js';
Q8Why are modules loaded only once?Show answer

Modules are cached by URL. Importing the same file from ten places runs its top-level code once and shares the same instance. This makes a module a natural singleton.

Q9What is a circular dependency and what problem can it cause?Show answer

When module A imports B and B imports A. One of them sees the other before it finishes running, so some values may still be uninitialized (TDZ errors). Fix by moving shared code into a third module.

JavaScript · Section 12

Symbol

Study notes

Symbol

The idea: Symbol() creates a brand-new, unique primitive value every time. Its main job is to be an object key that can never clash with any other key, which is great for adding hidden or "special" properties without breaking other code.

const ID = Symbol('id');           // 'id' is only a label for debugging
const user = { name: 'Asha', [ID]: 501 };
user[ID];                           // 501
Object.keys(user);                  // ['name'] - symbol key is skipped

const shared = Symbol.for('app.theme');      // global registry: same key -> same symbol
shared === Symbol.for('app.theme');           // true

Well-known symbols let your objects plug into language features:

Symbol Controls
Symbol.iterator how for...of and spread walk your object
Symbol.asyncIterator how for await...of works
Symbol.toPrimitive conversion to number/string
Symbol.toStringTag the [object X] name
Symbol.hasInstance how instanceof answers

Watch out: symbols are not fully private (Object.getOwnPropertySymbols finds them). Use #private fields for real privacy. Symbols can't be auto-converted with +; use String(sym) or sym.description.

Practice · 5 questions

Q1What is a Symbol and why was it added?Show answer

A Symbol is a primitive value that is always unique. It is mainly used as an object key that will never clash with other keys, even ones with the same description.

const a = Symbol('id');
const b = Symbol('id');
a === b;          // false - always unique
a.description;    // 'id'
Q2Are symbol-keyed properties hidden?Show answer

They are skipped by for...in, Object.keys and JSON.stringify, but they are not truly private. You can still read them with Object.getOwnPropertySymbols or Reflect.ownKeys.

const secret = Symbol('secret');
const user = { name: 'Asha', [secret]: 'xyz' };
Object.keys(user);                    // ['name']
JSON.stringify(user);                 // '{"name":"Asha"}'
Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(user);   // [Symbol(secret)]
Reflect.ownKeys(user);                // ['name', Symbol(secret)]
Q3Symbol() vs Symbol.for()?Show answer

Symbol() makes a new unique symbol every time. Symbol.for(key) looks in a global registry and returns the same symbol for the same key, even across files or iframes.

Symbol.for('app') === Symbol.for('app'); // true
Symbol.keyFor(Symbol.for('app'));        // 'app'
Symbol('app') === Symbol('app');         // false
Q4What are well-known symbols? Give examples.Show answer

Built-in symbols that let you change how the language treats your objects.

class Money {
  constructor(amount) { this.amount = amount; }
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {               // controls conversion
    return hint === 'string' ? `Rs ${this.amount}` : this.amount;
  }
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return 'Money'; }
}
const m = new Money(250);
`${m}`;                        // 'Rs 250'
m + 50;                        // 300
Object.prototype.toString.call(m); // '[object Money]'

Others: Symbol.iterator (for for...of), Symbol.asyncIterator, Symbol.hasInstance (custom instanceof).

Q5Can you use new Symbol()?Show answer

No, it throws a TypeError. Symbols are primitives, so there is no constructor call. Also, Symbol() + '' throws; you must convert with String(sym) or sym.toString().

JavaScript · Section 13

Collections (Map, Set)

Study notes

Map

The idea: A Map stores key–value pairs like an object, but keys can be any type (objects, numbers, functions), it remembers insertion order, it knows its size, and it can be looped directly. It is built for frequent adding and removing.

const stock = new Map([['pen', 10], ['book', 4]]);
stock.set('bag', 2);
stock.get('pen');      // 10
stock.has('book');     // true
stock.delete('bag');
stock.size;            // 2
for (const [item, qty] of stock) console.log(item, qty);
stock.forEach((qty, item) => console.log(item, qty));

Use Map when: keys are not strings, keys come from users (no clash with __proto__), or you add/remove often. Use an object for fixed records and JSON data (Maps don't JSON.stringify directly).

Set

The idea: A Set holds unique values: adding an existing value does nothing. Checking has is very fast, faster than array.includes for big lists.

const tags = new Set(['js', 'css']);
tags.add('js');          // ignored - already there
tags.add('html');
tags.has('css');         // true
tags.size;               // 3
[...tags];               // back to array

const uniqueIds = [...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])]; // [3, 1, 2]

Related: WeakMap / WeakSet take only objects as keys and let them be garbage-collected when nothing else uses them. They are not iterable. Use them to attach extra data to objects (like DOM nodes) without memory leaks.

Practice · 8 questions

Q1Map vs plain object: when would you use a Map?Show answer
Feature Object Map
Key types Strings and symbols only Any value (objects, functions, numbers)
Key order Mostly insertion (integers first) Always insertion order
Size Object.keys(o).length map.size
Iterable directly No Yes
Prototype keys risk Yes (e.g. 'constructor') No
Frequent add/delete Slower Built for it 
const visits = new Map();
const userObj = { id: 1 };
visits.set(userObj, 3);         // object as key
visits.get(userObj);            // 3
visits.has(userObj);            // true
for (const [user, count] of visits) console.log(user.id, count);
Q2Convert between Map and object / array.Show answer
const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
const map = new Map(Object.entries(obj));   // object -> Map
const back = Object.fromEntries(map);       // Map -> object
const arr = [...map];                       // [['a',1],['b',2]]
Q3What is a Set? Remove duplicates from an array.Show answer

A Set stores unique values only. Uniqueness uses "SameValueZero" (like ===, but NaN equals NaN).

const nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, NaN, NaN];
const unique = [...new Set(nums)];   // [1, 2, 3, NaN]
const s = new Set(['a']);
s.add('b').add('a');                 // chainable, 'a' ignored
s.size;                              // 2
Q4Do Sets treat two objects with the same content as duplicates?Show answer

No. Objects are compared by reference.

const s = new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
s.size; // 2
Q5Union, intersection and difference with Sets.Show answer
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
const b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);

// Newer built-in methods (ES2025)
a.union(b);         // {1, 2, 3, 4}
a.intersection(b);  // {2, 3}
a.difference(b);    // {1}

// Older way
const inter = new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)));
Q6What are WeakMap and WeakSet? Why use them?Show answer

Keys must be objects, and they are held weakly: if nothing else refers to the key, it can be garbage-collected. They are not iterable and have no size. Good for storing extra data about objects without causing memory leaks.

const metadata = new WeakMap();
function track(el) { metadata.set(el, { clicks: 0 }); }
let btn = document.querySelector('button');
track(btn);
btn = null; // entry can now be cleaned up automatically
Q7Count word frequency using a Map.Show answer
const text = 'the cat and the hat';
const freq = new Map();
for (const w of text.split(' ')) freq.set(w, (freq.get(w) ?? 0) + 1);
[...freq].sort((x, y) => y[1] - x[1])[0]; // ['the', 2]
Q8Build a simple LRU cache with a Map.Show answer

A Map keeps insertion order, so the first key is the oldest. On every read, delete and re-insert the key to mark it as recent.

class LRU {
  constructor(limit) { this.limit = limit; this.map = new Map(); }
  get(k) {
    if (!this.map.has(k)) return undefined;
    const v = this.map.get(k);
    this.map.delete(k); this.map.set(k, v);   // move to newest
    return v;
  }
  set(k, v) {
    this.map.delete(k);
    this.map.set(k, v);
    if (this.map.size > this.limit) this.map.delete(this.map.keys().next().value);
  }
}

JavaScript · Section 14

Error handling

Study notes

try...catch

The idea: Wrap risky code in try. If anything inside throws, JavaScript stops that block and jumps to catch, giving you the error object (with name, message and stack). The program keeps running instead of crashing.

function parseSettings(text) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text);
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn('Bad settings, using defaults:', err.message);
    return { theme: 'light' };
  }
}

Remember: try...catch only catches errors thrown while the try block is running. An error thrown later in a timer callback escapes it; for promises use await inside the try.

try...catch...finally

The idea: finally runs no matter what: after success, after an error, even after a return. Use it for cleanup like closing a connection or hiding a spinner.

async function upload(file) {
  showSpinner();
  try {
    await send(file);
    return 'ok';
  } catch (e) {
    return 'failed';
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();   // runs in both cases, before the value is returned
  }
}

Watch out: a return inside finally overrides the earlier return or error. Avoid returning from finally.

throw

The idea: throw raises your own error to stop normal flow and signal a problem to the caller. Throw Error objects (or subclasses) so a stack trace is included. Create custom classes for specific problems.

class InsufficientFundsError extends Error {
  constructor(needed) {
    super(`Need Rs ${needed} more`);
    this.name = 'InsufficientFundsError';
  }
}
function pay(balance, amount) {
  if (typeof amount !== 'number') throw new TypeError('Amount must be a number');
  if (amount > balance) throw new InsufficientFundsError(amount - balance);
  return balance - amount;
}

Built-in types to know: TypeError, RangeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, AggregateError.

Optional catch binding

The idea: Since ES2019 you can write catch { } without (err) when you don't need the error object.

let storageWorks = true;
try { localStorage.setItem('t', '1'); }
catch { storageWorks = false; }   // e.g. private mode

Practice · 9 questions

Q1How does try...catch work? What errors does it NOT catch?Show answer

Code in try runs; if it throws, control jumps to catch with the error. It does not catch syntax errors in the same script (the code never runs), and it does not catch errors thrown later inside callbacks such as setTimeout.

try {
  JSON.parse('{bad json}');
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name, err.message); // SyntaxError ...
}

try {
  setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('later'); }, 0);
} catch (e) {
  console.log('never runs');         // try already finished
}
Q2What are the built-in error types?Show answer

Error (base), SyntaxError, ReferenceError (unknown variable), TypeError (wrong type, e.g. calling undefined), RangeError (number out of range), URIError, EvalError, AggregateError (many errors, from Promise.any).

try { undefinedVar; } catch (e) { e instanceof ReferenceError; } // true
try { null.x; }       catch (e) { e instanceof TypeError; }      // true
try { new Array(-1); }catch (e) { e instanceof RangeError; }     // true
Q3When does finally run? What if both try and finally return?Show answer

finally always runs, after try or catch, even if they return. If finally itself returns, that value wins (avoid this).

function test() {
  try { return 'from try'; }
  finally { console.log('cleanup'); }
}
test(); // logs 'cleanup', returns 'from try'

function weird() {
  try { return 1; } finally { return 2; }
}
weird(); // 2
Q4How do you throw an error? Can you throw anything?Show answer

Use throw. You can throw any value, but always throw an Error object so you get a stack trace.

function withdraw(balance, amt) {
  if (amt > balance) throw new RangeError(`Need ${amt - balance} more`);
  return balance - amt;
}
throw 'oops';            // works, but no stack trace - bad practice
Q5Create a custom error class.Show answer
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
    this.field = field;
  }
}
try {
  throw new ValidationError('email', 'Email is required');
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof ValidationError) console.log(e.field, e.message);
  else throw e;           // re-throw errors you can't handle
}
Q6What is error cause?Show answer

When you wrap a low-level error in a higher-level one, pass the original as cause so the chain is not lost.

try {
  await fetch('/api');
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error('Could not load dashboard', { cause: err });
}
Q7What is optional catch binding?Show answer

You can leave out the error variable when you do not need it.

function isJSON(str) {
  try { JSON.parse(str); return true; }
  catch { return false; }       // no (err) needed
}
Q8How do you catch errors globally?Show answer
// Browser
window.addEventListener('error', e => console.log('Uncaught:', e.message));
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', e => console.log('Promise:', e.reason));

// Node
process.on('uncaughtException', err => { log(err); process.exit(1); });
process.on('unhandledRejection', reason => log(reason));
Q9Error-handling best practices to mention in an interviewShow answer
  • Throw Error objects, not strings.
  • Catch only what you can handle; re-throw the rest.
  • Never leave an empty catch {} that hides bugs silently.
  • Always end promise chains with .catch() or wrap await in try/catch.
  • Use finally for cleanup (close files, hide loaders, release locks).

JavaScript · Section 15

var, let and const

Study notes

let

The idea: let declares a variable that lives only inside the nearest { } block (block scope). It can be reassigned but not declared twice in the same block. It is hoisted, but touching it before its line throws an error (the Temporal Dead Zone).

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { /* i exists only here */ }
// console.log(i); // ReferenceError

let score = 10;
score = 20;        // ok
// let score = 30; // SyntaxError: already declared

let vs var

The idea: var is the old way, with surprising rules. The main differences:

var let
Scope whole function { } block
Before declaration undefined ReferenceError (TDZ)
Redeclare allowed error
In loops with callbacks one shared variable new variable each round
At top level becomes window.x does not 
if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2; }
a;  // 1 - leaked out of the block
// b -> ReferenceError

const

The idea: const is like let but must be given a value at once and can't be reassigned. It protects the variable binding, not the value inside: objects and arrays held in a const can still be changed.

const MAX_USERS = 100;
// MAX_USERS = 200;   // TypeError
const list = [];
list.push('a');       // allowed - same array, changed contents

Rule of thumb: use const by default, let when you must reassign, and avoid var.

Practice · 7 questions

Q1Compare var, let and const.Most askedShow answer
Feature var let const
Scope Function Block {} Block {}
Hoisted Yes, set to undefined Yes, but in TDZ Yes, but in TDZ
Re-declare in same scope Allowed Error Error
Re-assign Allowed Allowed Error
Adds to global object (window) Yes No No
Q2What is block scope? Show the difference.Show answer
if (true) {
  var a = 1;
  let b = 2;
}
console.log(a); // 1  - var ignores the block
console.log(b); // ReferenceError
Q3What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?Show answer

The time from the start of a block until the let/const line runs. The variable exists (it is hoisted) but you cannot touch it yet.

console.log(x); // undefined (var)
var x = 5;

console.log(y); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization
let y = 5;

let z = 'outer';
{
  console.log(z); // ReferenceError - inner z shadows outer, still in TDZ
  let z = 'inner';
}
Q4Does const make an object immutable?Show answer

No. const only stops you from pointing the variable at something else. The object itself can still change. Use Object.freeze to stop changes.

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
user.name = 'Ravi';   // allowed
// user = {};         // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
const frozen = Object.freeze({ n: 1 });
frozen.n = 2;         // ignored
Q5Why is let better in loops?Show answer

let creates a fresh binding for each loop round, so closures capture the right value. (See the setTimeout loop in Section 4, Q5.)

const fns = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
fns.map(f => f()); // [0, 1, 2]
Q6Must const be initialized?Show answer
const a;        // SyntaxError: Missing initializer
const b = 10;   // ok
Q7Which should you use by default?Show answer

Use const by default. Use let only when the value must change. Avoid var in new code. This makes intent clear and prevents accidental reassignment.

JavaScript · Section 16

Proxy & Reflect

Study notes

Proxy

The idea: new Proxy(target, handler) creates a stand-in object. Every basic action on it (read, write, delete, in, function call, new) can be caught by a trap in the handler, where you can change, check or log what happens before passing it to the real target. Think of a receptionist who sees every visitor before they reach the office.

const prices = { pen: 20, book: 150 };
const shop = new Proxy(prices, {
  get(target, item) {
    return item in target ? target[item] : 'Item not available';
  },
  set(target, item, value) {
    if (value < 0) throw new RangeError('Price cannot be negative');
    target[item] = value;
    return true;
  },
  deleteProperty() { throw new Error('Items cannot be removed'); }
});
shop.bag;        // 'Item not available'
shop.pen = 25;   // ok

Common uses: validation, default values, logging/debugging, read-only views, and reactivity in frameworks like Vue 3.

Watch out: set and deleteProperty traps must return true on success; returning false throws in strict mode. Proxies add some speed cost on hot paths.

Reflection (Reflect API)

The idea: Reflect is a built-in object with one method for each basic object action: Reflect.get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, defineProperty, apply, construct, getPrototypeOf... They do the normal default behaviour, and return true/false instead of throwing where possible. Inside a Proxy trap, Reflect is the clean way to say "now do the normal thing".

const audited = new Proxy({}, {
  set(target, key, value, receiver) {
    console.log(`set ${String(key)}`);
    return Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver); // default action + correct this
  }
});

Reflect.ownKeys({ a: 1, [Symbol('s')]: 2 }); // ['a', Symbol(s)] - all own keys
Reflect.construct(Date, [2026, 0, 1]);       // same as new Date(2026, 0, 1)
Reflect.has({ x: 1 }, 'x');                   // true

Practice · 7 questions

Q1What is a Proxy?Show answer

A Proxy wraps an object (the target) and lets you step in when someone reads, writes, deletes or checks its properties. The functions that step in are called traps, and they live in a handler object.

const target = { name: 'Asha' };
const handler = {
  get(obj, prop) {
    return prop in obj ? obj[prop] : `No property '${String(prop)}'`;
  }
};
const p = new Proxy(target, handler);
p.name; // 'Asha'
p.age;  // "No property 'age'"
Q2Use a Proxy to validate data.Show answer
const person = new Proxy({}, {
  set(obj, prop, value) {
    if (prop === 'age' && (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0)) {
      throw new TypeError('Age must be a positive integer');
    }
    obj[prop] = value;
    return true;         // must return true for success
  }
});
person.age = 30;   // ok
person.age = -5;   // TypeError
Q3Name common Proxy traps.Show answer

get, set, has (for in), deleteProperty, ownKeys, apply (calling a function), construct (new), defineProperty, getPrototypeOf.

Q4What is the Reflect API, and why use it with Proxy?Show answer

Reflect has one method for each trap, doing the default action. Inside a trap, calling Reflect.x(...) forwards the operation correctly (including the right this for getters) and returns a proper boolean.

const logged = new Proxy({ a: 1 }, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    console.log(`read ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);   // default behaviour
  },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) {
    console.log(`write ${String(prop)} = ${value}`);
    return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver);
  }
});
logged.a;      // read a
logged.b = 2;  // write b = 2
Q5Reflect vs Object methods: what is different?Show answer

Reflect methods return booleans instead of throwing in many cases, take functions as normal calls, and group all meta-operations in one place.

const frozen = Object.freeze({});
Reflect.defineProperty(frozen, 'x', { value: 1 });  // false (no throw)
Reflect.has({ a: 1 }, 'a');                         // true  (same as 'a' in obj)
Reflect.ownKeys({ a: 1, [Symbol('s')]: 2 });        // ['a', Symbol(s)]
Reflect.apply(Math.max, null, [1, 5, 3]);           // 5
Q6Real-world uses of Proxy?Show answer

Reactivity in frameworks (Vue 3 tracks reads and writes with Proxies), validation, default values, logging and debugging, read-only views, and negative array indexes.

const negArray = arr => new Proxy(arr, {
  get(t, p, r) {
    const i = Number(p);
    return Number.isInteger(i) && i < 0 ? t[t.length + i] : Reflect.get(t, p, r);
  }
});
negArray([10, 20, 30])[-1]; // 30
Q7Build a simple reactive (observable) object.Show answer
function reactive(obj, onChange) {
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    set(t, p, v, r) {
      const old = t[p];
      const ok = Reflect.set(t, p, v, r);
      if (old !== v) onChange(p, old, v);
      return ok;
    }
  });
}
const state = reactive({ count: 0 }, (k, o, n) => console.log(`${k}: ${o} -> ${n}`));
state.count++; // count: 0 -> 1

JavaScript · Section 17

JavaScript runtime

Study notes

Execution context

The idea: An execution context is the "room" where a piece of code runs. It holds that code's variables, its this, and a link to the outer room (for the scope chain). There is one global context when the script starts, and a new function context every time a function is called.

Each context is made in two phases:

  1. Creation: the engine scans the code and sets up memory. Function declarations are stored fully; var names get undefined; let/const names are noted but locked (TDZ); this is set.
  2. Execution: the code runs top to bottom, assigning values and calling functions.

This two-phase setup is the reason hoisting exists.

Call stack

The idea: The call stack is a to-do pile that tracks which function is running now. Calling a function pushes its context on top; returning pops it off. JavaScript always runs whatever is on top. Error stack traces are a printout of this pile.

function a() { b(); }
function b() { throw new Error('where am I?'); }
a();
// Error: where am I?
//   at b ...
//   at a ...
//   at <global>

Watch out: recursion with no exit fills the stack: "Maximum call stack size exceeded". A long-running function on the stack blocks the page from responding.

Event loop

The idea: JavaScript has one call stack, so how does it wait for timers and network without freezing? It hands slow jobs to the browser/Node (web APIs). When a job finishes, its callback is placed in a queue. The event loop keeps checking: "Is the call stack empty? Then take the next waiting callback."

There are two queues with different priority:

  • Microtask queue (high priority): promise .then/.catch/.finally, code after await, queueMicrotask. Fully emptied every time the stack empties.
  • Macrotask (task) queue: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, user events. One task per loop turn.
console.log('start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'));
console.log('end');
// start, end, promise, timeout

Rule to remember: sync code → all microtasks → (render) → one macrotask → repeat.

Hoisting

The idea: Because of the creation phase, declarations are known before the code runs, as if they were lifted to the top of their scope. Only the declaration is lifted, never the assignment.

Declaration Usable before its line?
function foo() {} Yes, fully
var x = 1 Yes, but value is undefined
let / const No, ReferenceError (TDZ)
class A {} No, ReferenceError (TDZ)
const f = () => {} No (it's a const)

Tip: declare things before using them; hoisting rules then never surprise you.

Variable scopes

The idea: Scope decides where a variable can be seen.

  • Global scope: visible everywhere (avoid putting much here).
  • Module scope: top level of a module file; private to that file.
  • Function scope: variables declared inside a function (var, let, const).
  • Block scope: let/const inside any { } (if, for, plain blocks).

JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function can see variables from where it was written, looking outward layer by layer (the scope chain). Inner can see outer; outer cannot see inner.

const app = 'Shop';
function outer() {
  const user = 'Asha';
  function inner() { return `${user} @ ${app}`; } // sees both
  return inner();
}
// console.log(user); // ReferenceError - outer can't see inside

Practice · 11 questions

Q1What is an execution context?Show answer

The environment where code runs. There is one global context, and a new function context each time a function is called. Each context is built in two phases:

  1. Creation phase: memory is set up. Function declarations are stored whole, var variables are set to undefined, let/const are registered but left in the TDZ, and this is decided.
  2. Execution phase: code runs line by line and values are assigned.
Q2What is the call stack?Show answer

A stack (last in, first out) that tracks which function is running. A call pushes a frame; a return pops it. Too many frames cause a stack overflow.

function a() { b(); }
function b() { c(); }
function c() { console.trace(); } // shows c <- b <- a <- global
a();

function forever() { forever(); }
// forever(); // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
Q3Explain the event loop.Most askedShow answer

JavaScript runs one thing at a time on the call stack. Slow work (timers, network, file I/O) is handed to the browser or Node. When that work finishes, its callback is put in a queue. The event loop repeats this cycle:

  1. Run all synchronous code until the call stack is empty.
  2. Run all microtasks (promise .then, await continuations, queueMicrotask).
  3. (Browser) render the page if needed.
  4. Take one macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events) and go back to step 1.
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);         // macrotask
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('C'));         // microtask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('D')); // microtask
console.log('E');
// A E C D B
Q4Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not run immediately?Show answer

0 is the minimum delay, not a promise to run now. The callback waits in the macrotask queue until the stack is empty and all microtasks are done. Browsers also clamp nested timers to about 4 ms.

Q5Can microtasks block the page?Show answer

Yes. The loop drains every microtask before rendering or taking the next macrotask. A microtask that keeps adding new microtasks freezes the page.

function loop() { Promise.resolve().then(loop); }
// loop(); // page freezes - timers and clicks never get a turn
Q6What is hoisting?Show answer

During the creation phase, declarations are registered before code runs, so it looks like they were "moved to the top". Only declarations are hoisted, not assignments.

console.log(typeof greet); // 'function' - fully hoisted
console.log(count);        // undefined - var hoisted, value not
console.log(typeof sayBye);// undefined - var hoisted, function expression not
function greet() {}
var count = 5;
var sayBye = () => {};
Q7Tricky hoisting questionShow answer
var x = 1;
function show() {
  console.log(x); // undefined, not 1
  var x = 2;      // local x is hoisted inside show()
}
show();
Q8What are the kinds of scope in JavaScript?Show answer

Global scope, module scope, function scope, and block scope (let/const inside {}). JavaScript uses lexical scope: what a function can see depends on where it is written, not where it is called.

const who = 'global';
function outer() {
  const who = 'outer';
  function inner() { return who; }   // looks outward when written
  return inner;
}
const fn = outer();
fn(); // 'outer'
Q9What is the scope chain?Show answer

When a variable is used, the engine looks in the current scope, then the parent scope, and so on up to global. If it is not found, a ReferenceError is thrown. Inner scopes can see outer ones, never the other way.

Q10What is variable shadowing?Show answer
let level = 'outer';
{
  let level = 'inner';   // shadows the outer one in this block
  console.log(level);    // 'inner'
}
console.log(level);      // 'outer'
Q11What causes memory leaks in JavaScript?Show answer

Values stay in memory while something still refers to them. Common causes: forgotten timers, event listeners never removed, accidental globals, large data kept alive by closures, and detached DOM nodes still stored in variables.

const id = setInterval(poll, 1000);
// later, when the component is removed:
clearInterval(id);
el.removeEventListener('click', handler);

JavaScript · Section 18

Primitive wrapper types

Study notes

Primitive wrapper types

The idea: Primitives (string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol) are not objects, yet you can call 'hi'.toUpperCase(). That works because JavaScript quietly wraps the primitive in a temporary object (String, Number, Boolean...), runs the method, then throws the wrapper away. null and undefined have no wrappers, so calling a method on them throws.

Remember: call String(x), Number(x), Boolean(x) without new to convert values. With new you get an object, which behaves strangely (new Boolean(false) is truthy).

Boolean type

The idea: Boolean(value) (or !!value) converts anything to true/false using the truthy/falsy rules. The wrapper adds almost nothing useful beyond toString() and valueOf().

const names = ['Asha', '', null, 'Ravi'];
names.filter(Boolean);  // ['Asha', 'Ravi'] - quick way to drop falsy values

Number type

The idea: The Number wrapper gives formatting methods and static helpers.

const price = 1234.567;
price.toFixed(2);                 // '1234.57'  (string!)
price.toPrecision(3);             // '1.23e+3'
price.toLocaleString('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }); // '₹1,234.57'
Number('42');                     // 42
Number('42px');                   // NaN
parseInt('42px', 10);             // 42 - reads until it can't
Number.isInteger(4.0);            // true
Number.EPSILON;                   // smallest useful difference

Watch out: toFixed returns a string; convert back with Number() before more math.

BigInt

The idea: bigint is a primitive for whole numbers of any size. Add n to a literal (123n) or call BigInt('123'). Use it when numbers go beyond 2^53 − 1 and must stay exact.

const huge = 2n ** 100n;     // exact
huge + 1n;
5n / 2n;                     // 2n - drops the fraction
// 1n + 1;                   // TypeError: can't mix with number
BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) + 2n; // exact, unlike number

Watch out: Math methods don't accept BigInt, and JSON.stringify throws on BigInt (convert to string first).

String type

The idea: The String wrapper provides the methods you use daily. All of them return new strings; the original never changes.

Task Method
Search includes, indexOf, startsWith, endsWith, search
Cut slice, substring, at, charAt
Change case toUpperCase, toLowerCase
Clean trim, trimStart, trimEnd
Split / join split (string → array), array.join
Replace replace, replaceAll
Pad / repeat padStart, padEnd, repeat
Compare localeCompare 
const email = '  Asha@Mail.com ';
email.trim().toLowerCase();               // 'asha@mail.com'
'2026-10-12'.split('-');                   // ['2026', '10', '12']
'7'.padStart(3, '0');                     // '007'

Practice · 8 questions

Q1How can a primitive string have methods like .toUpperCase()?Show answer

When you call a method on a primitive, JavaScript briefly wraps it in a wrapper object (String, Number, Boolean), calls the method, then throws the wrapper away. This is called auto-boxing.

const s = 'hello';
s.toUpperCase();  // 'HELLO' - temporary String object used
s.extra = 1;      // set on the temporary wrapper
s.extra;          // undefined - wrapper is already gone
Q2Why should you avoid new String(), new Number(), new Boolean()?Show answer

They create objects, not primitives, which breaks typeof, equality and conditions.

const a = 'hi';
const b = new String('hi');
typeof b;           // 'object'
a === b;            // false
if (new Boolean(false)) console.log('runs!'); // objects are always truthy
String(123);        // '123' - without new: safe conversion
Q3Useful Number methods to know.Show answer
(3.14159).toFixed(2);       // '3.14' (string, rounded)
(1234.5).toLocaleString('en-IN'); // '1,234.5'
Number.isInteger(5.0);      // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2**53);// false
Number.parseFloat('3.5kg'); // 3.5
parseInt('08', 10);         // 8 - always pass the radix
Number('12px');             // NaN - Number() is stricter than parseInt
Q4What is BigInt? When do you need it?Show answer

A primitive for whole numbers of any size, written with an n suffix. Use it beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (IDs from databases, crypto, exact big math).

const big = 9007199254740993n;
big + 1n;          // 9007199254740994n
// big + 1;        // TypeError: cannot mix BigInt and Number
Number(big) + 1;   // converts, may lose precision
7n / 2n;           // 3n - division drops the decimal
typeof 10n;        // 'bigint'
1n == 1;           // true
1n === 1;          // false (different types)
Q5Common String methods asked in interviews.Show answer
const s = '  JavaScript Rocks  ';
s.trim();                    // 'JavaScript Rocks'
s.includes('Script');        // true
s.trim().startsWith('Java'); // true
s.indexOf('a');              // 3
s.trim().split(' ');         // ['JavaScript', 'Rocks']
'ab'.repeat(3);              // 'ababab'
'5'.padStart(3, '0');        // '005'
'a-b-c'.replaceAll('-', '/');// 'a/b/c'
'hello'.at(-1);              // 'o'
Q6slice vs substring vs substr?Show answer

slice(start, end) supports negative indexes. substring(start, end) treats negatives as 0 and swaps arguments if start > end. substr(start, length) is deprecated; avoid it.

'JavaScript'.slice(-6);        // 'Script'
'JavaScript'.substring(4, 0);  // 'Java' (swapped)
Q7Reverse a string and check for a palindrome.Show answer
const reverse = s => [...s].reverse().join('');  // spread handles emoji
const isPalindrome = s => {
  const clean = s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '');
  return clean === reverse(clean);
};
isPalindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'); // true
Q8How do template literals and tagged templates work?Show answer
const name = 'Asha', score = 92;
`Hi ${name}, you scored ${score >= 90 ? 'A' : 'B'}`; // expressions inside

function highlight(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((out, str, i) =>
    out + str + (i < values.length ? `[${values[i]}]` : ''), '');
}
highlight`User ${name} scored ${score}`; // 'User [Asha] scored [92]'

JavaScript · Section 19

Advanced operators

Study notes

Logical assignment operators

The idea: Three shortcuts that assign only when a condition holds. They combine a logical operator with =.

Operator Assigns when the left side is Same idea as
a ||= b falsy a || (a = b)
a &&= b truthy a && (a = b)
a ??= b null or undefined a ?? (a = b) 
const options = { timeout: 0, retries: null };
options.timeout ??= 3000;  // stays 0 (0 is a real value)
options.retries ??= 3;     // becomes 3
let message = '';
message ||= 'No message';  // '' is falsy -> replaced

Nullish coalescing operator (??)

The idea: a ?? b returns a unless a is null or undefined; then it returns b. It is the safe way to give default values, because it keeps valid falsy values like 0, '' and false, which || would wrongly replace.

const qty = 0;
qty || 1;   // 1  - wrong for a real zero
qty ?? 1;   // 0  - correct
const name = user?.name ?? 'Guest';  // pairs well with ?.

Rule: you can't mix ?? with && / || without brackets.

Exponentiation operator (**)

The idea: a ** b means "a to the power of b", the same as Math.pow(a, b). It works with BigInt too, and has the compound form **=.

3 ** 2;          // 9
2 ** -1;         // 0.5
9 ** 0.5;        // 3 (square root)
2 ** 3 ** 2;     // 512 - evaluated right to left: 2 ** 9
let area = 4; area **= 2; // 16
// -2 ** 2;      // SyntaxError: write (-2) ** 2

Practice · 8 questions

Q1What is the nullish coalescing operator ??, and how is it different from ||?Show answer

?? returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined. || returns the right side for any falsy value, which wrongly replaces valid values like 0, '' and false.

const settings = { volume: 0, title: '', darkMode: false };
settings.volume || 50;    // 50  - wrong, 0 was a real value
settings.volume ?? 50;    // 0   - correct
settings.title ?? 'Untitled'; // ''
settings.missing ?? 'default'; // 'default'
Q2Can you mix ?? with && or ||?Show answer

Not without parentheses; it is a SyntaxError, to avoid confusion.

// a || b ?? c;       // SyntaxError
(a || b) ?? c;        // ok
Q3What are logical assignment operators?Show answer

Short forms that assign only under a condition:

  • a ||= b → assign if a is falsy.
  • a &&= b → assign if a is truthy.
  • a ??= b → assign if a is null or undefined.
const opts = { retries: 0, name: null, token: 'abc' };
opts.retries ||= 3;   // 3   (0 is falsy)
opts.name ??= 'guest';// 'guest'
opts.token &&= opts.token.toUpperCase(); // 'ABC'

const cache = {};
(cache.users ??= []).push('Asha'); // create array once, then use it
Q4How is a ??= b different from a = a ?? b?Show answer

??= short-circuits: if a already has a value, no assignment happens at all. This matters for setters and read-only properties.

Q5What is the exponentiation operator ``?Show answer

It raises a number to a power, like Math.pow. It is right-associative, and a unary minus on the left needs parentheses.

2 ** 10;       // 1024
2 ** 3 ** 2;   // 512 (= 2 ** 9, right to left)
(-2) ** 2;     // 4
// -2 ** 2;    // SyntaxError: ambiguous
4 ** 0.5;      // 2 (square root)
2n ** 64n;     // works with BigInt too
Q6Combine optional chaining and nullish coalescing for safe defaults.Show answer
const res = { data: { user: null } };
const city = res.data?.user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown';
console.log(city); // 'Unknown'
Q7What are bitwise operators used for in real code?Show answer

Flags and permissions, fast integer tricks, and low-level data. They convert numbers to 32-bit integers first.

const READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4;   // 001, 010, 100
let perms = READ | WRITE;              // 011
(perms & WRITE) !== 0;                 // true - has write
perms &= ~WRITE;                       // remove write
7 >> 1;                                // 3 (divide by 2, floor)
~~4.7;                                 // 4 (truncate)
Q8Quick recap: which default operator should you pick?Show answer
Want a default when the value is... Use
null or undefined only ?? / ??=
Any falsy value (0, '', false, NaN too) || / ||=
Missing deep inside an object ?. then ??

TypeScript

TypeScript · Section 1

Getting started

Study notes

What is TypeScript

The idea: TypeScript is JavaScript plus types. You write .ts files with type labels (let age: number), and the TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks them, then removes the types and outputs plain JavaScript. Browsers and Node never see the types; they only run the JavaScript. Microsoft created it in 2012.

Remember:

  • Every valid JavaScript file is (almost) valid TypeScript; you can adopt it file by file.
  • Types exist only at compile time. At run time there is no type checking at all.
  • TypeScript can output older JavaScript (e.g. ES5) from modern syntax.

Setting up the environment

The idea: You need Node.js, the TypeScript compiler and an editor (VS Code has TypeScript support built in).

npm install -D typescript     # add compiler to the project
npx tsc --init                 # create tsconfig.json
npx tsc                        # compile every .ts file per tsconfig
npx tsc --watch                # recompile on every save
npx tsx app.ts                 # run a .ts file directly (dev helper)

tsconfig.json settings to know: target (JS version to output), module, strict (turn on all strict checks; always use it), outDir, rootDir, noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks.

Hello World

// hello.ts
const message: string = 'Hello, World!';
console.log(message);

Run npx tsc hello.ts to get hello.js, then node hello.js. Open hello.js and notice : string is gone; that's the compile step removing types.

Why TypeScript

The idea: JavaScript only tells you about many mistakes when the code runs (often in front of users). TypeScript finds them while you type.

function getTotal(price: number, qty: number) { return price * qty; }
getTotal('100', 2);    // error in editor: string is not assignable to number

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
user.nmae;             // error: Property 'nmae' does not exist. Did you mean 'name'?

Benefits: fewer runtime bugs, better auto-complete, safe refactoring (rename across files), types act as live documentation, and large teams can understand each other's code. Cost: a build step and some learning.

Practice · 8 questions

Q1What is TypeScript, and how is it related to JavaScript?Show answer

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static types. It compiles (transpiles) to plain JavaScript, so it runs anywhere JavaScript runs. Types are checked at compile time and erased in the output.

Q2Does TypeScript check types at run time?Show answer

No. All types are removed during compilation. If data from an API has the wrong shape, TypeScript cannot catch it at run time. You need runtime validation (e.g. checks or a library like Zod) for outside data.

interface User { name: string }
const u = JSON.parse('{"name": 42}') as User; // compiles fine
u.name.toUpperCase();                         // crashes at run time
Q3Why would a team choose TypeScript over JavaScript?Show answer

It catches bugs before the code runs, gives strong editor auto-complete, makes refactoring safe, and types serve as documentation. The trade-offs are a build step, a learning curve and some extra code.

Q4What is tsconfig.json? Name important options.Show answer

The project's compiler settings file. Key options:

Option What it does
target JavaScript version to output (e.g. ES2022)
module / moduleResolution module system and how imports are found
strict turns on all strict checks (recommended)
outDir / rootDir where output goes / where source lives
noEmit type-check only (when a bundler builds)
lib built-in API types available (DOM, ES2023...)
Q5What does strict: true turn on?Show answer

A group of checks, the most important being noImplicitAny (no silent any), strictNullChecks (null/undefined must be handled), strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization (class fields must be set), and useUnknownInCatchVariables.

Q6What is the difference between tsc, ts-node/tsx, and a bundler like Vite or esbuild?Show answer

tsc type-checks and compiles. ts-node/tsx run .ts files directly for development. Bundlers like Vite/esbuild strip types very fast but do not type-check, so projects usually run tsc --noEmit separately in CI.

Q7Can TypeScript be used with existing JavaScript code?Show answer

Yes. Set allowJs: true to mix files, add // @ts-check to a JS file to check it using JSDoc comments, and migrate file by file. Libraries without types get them from @types/... packages or .d.ts files.

Q8Walk through compiling and running a Hello World TypeScript program. What changes in the output?Show answer
// hello.ts
const greet = (name: string): string => `Hello, ${name}!`;
console.log(greet('World'));

A: Run npx tsc hello.ts to produce hello.js, then node hello.js. In the output, the : string annotations are gone, and modern syntax may be rewritten to match target. If you call greet(42), tsc reports an error, but by default it still writes the JS file (use noEmitOnError to stop that).
