TypeScript · Section 2

Basic types

Study notes

TypeScript types (overview)

The idea: A type describes what values something can hold and what you can do with it. TypeScript has the JavaScript primitives (string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined) plus extra ones: any, unknown, never, void, tuples, enums, unions, literal types and more. Types are structural: two types match if their shapes match, no matter their names.

Type annotations

The idea: Write : Type after a name to declare its type. Use it for variables, function parameters and return values.

let city: string = 'Hyderabad';
let scores: number[] = [90, 85];
function area(w: number, h: number): number { return w * h; }
const user: { name: string; age: number } = { name: 'Ravi', age: 30 };

Type inference

The idea: You don't have to annotate everything. TypeScript works out (infers) types from values and return statements. Annotate function parameters and public APIs; let inference handle local variables.

let count = 5;          // inferred number
count = 'five';          // error
const role = 'admin';    // inferred as the literal type 'admin' (const can't change)
const nums = [1, 2, 3];  // number[]
function double(n: number) { return n * 2; } // return inferred as number

Watch out: let x; with no value starts as any-like. Give it a type or a value.

Number type

The idea: number covers integers and decimals (all floating point). bigint is a separate type for huge whole numbers; you can't mix them.

let price: number = 99.5;
let big: bigint = 9007199254740993n;
// price + big;  // error: can't mix number and bigint

Tip: use lowercase number, not Number (the wrapper object type).

String type

The idea: string holds text in single quotes, double quotes or template literals.

const first: string = 'Asha';
const greeting: string = `Hello ${first}`;

Boolean type

The idea: boolean is only true or false. TypeScript won't let other values sneak in, unlike JavaScript's truthy/falsy.

let isActive: boolean = true;
// isActive = 1;  // error

Null type

The idea: With strictNullChecks on, null and undefined are their own types. A string variable cannot hold null unless you say so with a union. This removes the classic "cannot read property of null" crash.

let middleName: string | null = null;
function len(s: string | null) {
  return s?.length ?? 0;      // must handle null first
}
const el = document.getElementById('app'); // HTMLElement | null
el!.textContent = 'hi';       // ! = "trust me, not null" (use rarely)

Object type

The idea: Describe an object's shape: property names and their types. Use ? for optional properties and readonly for properties that can't change. The lowercase object type means "any non-primitive" and is rarely useful.

let product: { readonly id: number; name: string; discount?: number };
product = { id: 1, name: 'Pen' };     // discount is optional
// product.id = 2;                     // error: readonly

Watch out: passing an object literal with an extra property is an error ("excess property check"), which catches typos.

Array type

The idea: Type[] or Array<Type> is a list where every item has that type. readonly Type[] blocks changes.

const names: string[] = ['a', 'b'];
const ids: Array<number> = [1, 2];
const mixed: (string | number)[] = ['a', 1];
const frozen: readonly string[] = ['x'];
// frozen.push('y');  // error

Tuple types

The idea: A tuple is an array with a fixed length where each position has its own type. Great for pairs like coordinates or [value, setValue].

let point: [number, number] = [10, 20];
let entry: [name: string, age: number] = ['Asha', 25]; // labeled
let withOptional: [string, number?] = ['only name'];
function useToggle(): [boolean, () => void] { /* ... */ return [true, () => {}]; }

Union types

The idea: A | B means "either A or B". Before using type-specific methods, you must check which one you have (narrowing).

function formatId(id: string | number) {
  if (typeof id === 'string') return id.toUpperCase(); // here: string
  return id.toFixed(0);                                // here: number
}

String literal types

The idea: A type that allows only exact string values. Combined with unions, they make a safe list of options (often better than enums).

type Size = 'S' | 'M' | 'L';
let shirt: Size = 'M';
// shirt = 'XL';  // error
function move(dir: 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right') {}

Unknown type

The idea: unknown can hold anything, like any, but you must check the type before using it. It is the safe choice for values you don't control (API data, JSON.parse, caught errors).

function handle(input: unknown) {
  // input.toUpperCase();          // error: check first
  if (typeof input === 'string') return input.toUpperCase();
  if (input instanceof Date) return input.toISOString();
  return String(input);
}

Any type

The idea: any switches off type checking for that value. Anything goes, and nothing is checked, so bugs slip through and spread to other variables. Use it only as a temporary escape hatch while migrating JavaScript.

let data: any = 'hello';
data.notAMethod();   // no error now, crash at run time

Rule: prefer unknown over any.

Enum types

The idea: An enum gives names to a set of related constants. Numeric enums count up from 0 by default; string enums need explicit values. Unlike most TypeScript features, enums create real JavaScript objects.

enum Status { Pending, Shipped, Delivered }        // 0, 1, 2
enum Color { Red = 'RED', Green = 'GREEN' }
let s: Status = Status.Shipped;
Status[1];   // 'Shipped' - numeric enums map both ways

Alternative many teams prefer: a union of string literals, or as const objects.

Void type

The idea: void is the return type of a function that doesn't return a useful value.

function log(msg: string): void { console.log(msg); }

Never type

The idea: never means "this can never happen": a function that always throws or loops forever, or a branch that's impossible. Its best use is exhaustive checks: if a new option is added to a union and not handled, you get a compile error.

type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'square'; s: number };
function area(sh: Shape): number {
  switch (sh.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * sh.r ** 2;
    case 'square': return sh.s ** 2;
    default:
      const unhandled: never = sh;   // error if a new kind is added
      throw new Error(`Unknown shape ${unhandled}`);
  }
}

Type aliases

The idea: type Name = ... gives a reusable name to any type: objects, unions, tuples, functions.

type ID = string | number;
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
type Callback = (err: Error | null, data?: string) => void;

Practice · 17 questions

Q1Type annotation vs type inference: when should you annotate?Show answer

Annotate function parameters, public function return types, and empty variables. Let inference handle local variables that get a value right away; extra annotations add noise.

const total = 100;                       // inferred, no annotation needed
function tax(amount: number): number {   // annotate inputs and outputs
  return amount * 0.18;
}
let result: string;                      // no value yet -> annotate
Q2Why does const x = 'hi' get type 'hi' but let y = 'hi' gets string?Show answer

A const can never change, so TypeScript infers the narrowest literal type. A let can be reassigned, so it widens to string. as const freezes literals in objects and arrays too.

const roles = ['admin', 'user'] as const; // readonly ['admin', 'user']
type Role = typeof roles[number];          // 'admin' | 'user'
Q3any vs unknown: what is the difference?Most askedShow answer

Both accept any value. any turns off checking: you can call anything on it, and it spreads silently. unknown forces you to narrow the type before use. Prefer unknown for untrusted data.

let a: any = 'x';     a.foo.bar();       // compiles, crashes later
let u: unknown = 'x'; // u.toUpperCase(); // error
if (typeof u === 'string') u.toUpperCase(); // ok after check
Q4void vs never vs undefined?Show answer

void: a function returns nothing useful (it still returns undefined). never: a function never finishes normally (always throws or loops), or a value that cannot exist. undefined: the actual value undefined.

function log(m: string): void { console.log(m); }
function fail(m: string): never { throw new Error(m); }
Q5How do you use never for exhaustive checking?Show answer
type Payment = 'card' | 'upi' | 'cash';
function fee(p: Payment) {
  switch (p) {
    case 'card': return 2;
    case 'upi': return 0;
    case 'cash': return 0;
    default: {
      const check: never = p;  // if 'wallet' is added later, this line errors
      return check;
    }
  }
}
Q6What is a tuple, and how is it different from an array?Show answer

A tuple has a fixed length and a type per position. An array has any length and one type for all items.

const rgb: [number, number, number] = [255, 0, 0];
// rgb[3];             // error: no index 3
const list: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4];

Watch out: push is still allowed on normal tuples; use readonly [number, number] to fully lock them.

Q7What are union types, and what is narrowing?Show answer

A union A | B allows either type. Narrowing is checking which one you have (typeof, instanceof, in, equality), after which TypeScript knows the exact type in that branch.

function print(v: string | string[]) {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return v.join(', '); // string[]
  return v;                                   // string
}
Q8Enums vs string literal unions: which would you choose?Show answer

String literal unions are lighter: no generated JavaScript, simple values, and they work well with JSON. Enums add a runtime object (useful if you need to loop over values) and give names to numbers. Many modern codebases prefer unions or as const objects.

enum Dir { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }          // creates a JS object
type Dir2 = 'UP' | 'DOWN';                      // erased at compile time
const DIR = { Up: 'UP', Down: 'DOWN' } as const;
type Dir3 = typeof DIR[keyof typeof DIR];       // 'UP' | 'DOWN'
Q9What is a const enum?Show answer

An enum whose uses are replaced with the literal values at compile time, so no object is generated. Smaller output, but you can't loop over it, and some build tools (isolated modules) don't support it.

Q10What does strictNullChecks change?Show answer

Without it, null and undefined can go into any type, hiding crashes. With it, they must be part of the type (string | null) and handled before use.

function greet(name: string | null) {
  // return name.toUpperCase();         // error: possibly null
  return name ? name.toUpperCase() : 'GUEST';
}
Q11What is the non-null assertion !, and why be careful?Show answer

value! tells the compiler "this is not null/undefined". It removes the check without any runtime protection, so if you're wrong, it crashes. Prefer real checks or ?..

Q12What is an excess property check?Show answer

When you assign an object literal directly to a typed variable, extra unknown properties are errors (they're probably typos). Assigning through another variable skips this check.

type Opts = { color?: string };
const a: Opts = { colour: 'red' };       // error: did you mean 'color'?
const raw = { colour: 'red' };
const b: Opts = raw;                      // allowed (no literal check)
Q13object vs Object vs {}?Show answer

object means any non-primitive. {} and Object mean "any value except null/undefined" (even strings and numbers). For real shapes, write the properties or use Record<string, unknown>.

Q14type alias vs interface?Most askedShow answer
type interface
Object shapes Yes Yes
Unions, tuples, primitives Yes No
Extend & intersection extends
Declaration merging (reopen later) No Yes
Mapped / conditional types Yes No

A: Use interface for object shapes and public APIs (can be extended and merged); use type for unions, tuples and computed types. Being consistent matters more than the choice.

Q15What is structural typing?Show answer

TypeScript compares types by their shape, not their name. If an object has all required properties with the right types, it fits, even if it was never declared with that type.

interface Point { x: number; y: number }
const p = { x: 1, y: 2, label: 'A' };
function draw(pt: Point) {}
draw(p);  // ok: p has x and y
Q16number vs Number, string vs String: which should you use?Show answer

Always the lowercase primitive types (number, string, boolean, bigint, symbol). The capitalized ones are the wrapper object types; they accept odd values like new String('x') and cause confusing errors.

let ok: string = 'hi';
let bad: String = new String('hi');   // works, but avoid
// ok = bad;                           // error: String is not string
let big: bigint = 10n;                  // separate from number
Q17How do you type arrays, and how do you stop an array from being changed?Show answer

T[] or Array<T> for normal arrays; readonly T[] or ReadonlyArray<T> removes push, pop, splice and index assignment. Readonly arrays are great for function parameters you promise not to modify.

function total(prices: readonly number[]) {
  // prices.push(1);     // error
  return prices.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
const matrix: number[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
const mixed: Array<string | number> = ['a', 1];

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 3

Control flow

Study notes

Overview

The idea: if...else, switch, for, while, do...while, break and continue work exactly as in JavaScript (see the JavaScript notes, Section 4). The TypeScript difference is control flow analysis: the compiler follows your conditions and narrows types inside each branch.

function describe(x: string | number | null) {
  if (x === null) return 'nothing';          // here x: null
  if (typeof x === 'number') return x.toFixed(2); // here x: number
  return x.trim();                            // here x: string
}

if...else

Conditions narrow types. After an early return, TypeScript remembers the removed case for the rest of the function.

switch...case

Switching on a literal union or a shared kind field narrows each case. Add a default with never to make sure every case is handled.

type Event = { type: 'click'; x: number } | { type: 'key'; key: string };
function handle(e: Event) {
  switch (e.type) {
    case 'click': return e.x;      // e is the click type
    case 'key': return e.key;      // e is the key type
  }
}

for, while, do...while

Loop variables are typed by inference (for (let i = 0; ...) gives number). With for...of, the item type comes from the array type.

break and continue

Same behaviour as JavaScript; labels work too. TypeScript flags code after an unconditional break/return as unreachable when allowUnreachableCode is false.

Practice · 5 questions

Q1What is control flow analysis (narrowing) in TypeScript?Show answer

The compiler follows if, switch, return, throw and loops, and narrows a variable's type in each branch based on the checks you wrote.

function len(v: string | string[] | undefined) {
  if (!v) return 0;                 // removes undefined (and '')
  if (typeof v === 'string') return v.length;
  return v.reduce((n, s) => n + s.length, 0); // v: string[]
}
Q2What narrowing checks does TypeScript understand?Show answer

typeof (primitives), instanceof (classes), in (property exists), equality (=== null, literal values), truthiness, Array.isArray, discriminant fields (kind/type), and custom type guard functions.

Q3What is a discriminated union, and why does switch work so well with it?Show answer

A union where every member has a common literal field (like status). Switching on that field narrows to exactly one member per case.

type Result =
  | { status: 'ok'; data: string[] }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string };
function show(r: Result) {
  switch (r.status) {
    case 'ok': return r.data.length;
    case 'error': return r.message;
  }
}
Q4Why can narrowing be lost inside a callback?Show answer

For a let variable, TypeScript can't be sure it wasn't changed before the callback runs, so it resets the narrowing. Copy it into a const first.

let name: string | null = getName();
if (name) {
  const safe = name;
  setTimeout(() => console.log(safe.toUpperCase()), 0); // ok
}
Q5How does TypeScript type the loop variable in for...of and for...in?Show answer

In for...of, it is the array's item type. In for...in, the key is always string (because objects may have extra keys), so indexing a typed object needs keyof or a cast.

const prices = { pen: 10, book: 50 };
for (const k in prices) {
  // prices[k];                               // error: string can't index
  prices[k as keyof typeof prices];           // ok
}

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 4

Functions

Study notes

Functions

The idea: Type each parameter, and optionally the return value. TypeScript then checks every call: the number of arguments and their types.

function formatPrice(amount: number, currency: string): string {
  return `${currency} ${amount.toFixed(2)}`;
}
formatPrice(99, 'INR');   // ok
// formatPrice(99);        // error: expected 2 arguments
const add = (a: number, b: number): number => a + b;

Function types

The idea: A function type describes a function's shape: (params) => returnType. Use it for callbacks and for variables that hold functions.

type Validator = (value: string) => boolean;
const notEmpty: Validator = v => v.trim().length > 0; // v inferred as string
function runAll(value: string, rules: Validator[]) {
  return rules.every(rule => rule(value));
}

Optional parameters

The idea: Add ? after a parameter name to make it optional. Its type becomes Type | undefined, so check it before use. Optional parameters must come after required ones.

function greet(name: string, title?: string) {
  return title ? `Hello ${title} ${name}` : `Hello ${name}`;
}

Default parameters

The idea: Give a fallback value; the type is inferred from it and the parameter becomes optional for callers.

function paginate(page = 1, size = 20) { /* page: number */ }
paginate();

Rest parameters

The idea: ...name: Type[] collects remaining arguments into a typed array.

function sum(...nums: number[]): number {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
sum(1, 2, 3);

Function overloading

The idea: Write several signatures (the outside promises) followed by one implementation that handles all of them. Callers see only the signatures, so each input type maps to a precise output type.

function parse(value: string): number;
function parse(value: number): string;
function parse(value: string | number): number | string {
  return typeof value === 'string' ? Number(value) : String(value);
}
const n = parse('42');  // n: number
const s = parse(42);    // s: string

Tip: if a union parameter is enough, skip overloads; they add complexity.

Practice · 8 questions

Q1How do you type a function and a callback?Show answer
function fetchUser(id: number, onDone: (user: { name: string }) => void): void {
  onDone({ name: 'Asha' });
}
type Handler = (event: MouseEvent) => void;
Q2Optional parameter vs default parameter vs param: T | undefined?Show answer

p?: T can be left out by the caller. p = value can be left out and gets a fallback. p: T | undefined must still be passed (even as undefined).

function a(x?: number) {}            a();   // ok
function b(x = 5) {}                  b();   // ok, x = 5
function c(x: number | undefined) {}  // c(); error, c(undefined) ok
Q3What is function overloading in TypeScript, and how is it different from Java?Show answer

You write several signatures and one implementation body; there is only one function at run time. In Java each overload has its own body. The implementation signature is not visible to callers.

function getItem(id: number): Product;
function getItem(ids: number[]): Product[];
function getItem(x: number | number[]): Product | Product[] {
  return Array.isArray(x) ? x.map(load) : load(x);
}
Q4Why does a callback typed to return void accept a function that returns a value?Show answer

A void return type in a function type means "the return value will be ignored", not "must return nothing". This lets you pass arr.push style functions to forEach.

const names: string[] = [];
['a', 'b'].forEach(n => names.push(n)); // push returns number, still ok
Q5How do you type this inside a function?Show answer

Add a fake first parameter named this. It is removed in output and checked at every call.

function onClick(this: HTMLButtonElement) { this.disabled = true; }
button.addEventListener('click', onClick);
Q6How do you type rest parameters and tuples together?Show answer
function log(level: 'info' | 'warn', ...parts: (string | number)[]) {}
function point(...coords: [number, number]) {}  // exactly 2 args
point(1, 2);
Q7What are Parameters<F> and ReturnType<F>?Show answer

Built-in utility types that pull out a function's parameter tuple and return type, so you don't repeat types.

function createOrder(id: number, items: string[]) { return { id, items, total: 0 }; }
type Args = Parameters<typeof createOrder>;   // [id: number, items: string[]]
type Order = ReturnType<typeof createOrder>;  // { id: number; items: string[]; total: number }
Q8What is the return type of an async function?Show answer

Always Promise<T>. Write async function load(): Promise<User>; Awaited<T> unwraps a promise type.

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 5

Classes

Study notes

Classes

The idea: TypeScript classes are JavaScript classes plus types. You must declare each property and its type at the top of the class (or via parameter properties). With strict, every property must be set in the constructor or given a default.

class Product {
  name: string;
  price: number;
  constructor(name: string, price: number) {
    this.name = name;
    this.price = price;
  }
  withTax(rate = 0.18): number { return this.price * (1 + rate); }
}

Shortcut (parameter properties): add a modifier to a constructor parameter to declare and assign it in one go.

class Product {
  constructor(public name: string, private price: number) {}
}

Access modifiers

The idea: Control who can use a member.

Modifier Visible in the class In subclasses Outside
public (default) Yes Yes Yes
protected Yes Yes No
private Yes No No

Watch out: these are compile-time only. At run time the property is still there. For real runtime privacy use JavaScript's #field.

readonly modifier

The idea: A readonly property can be set only where it is declared or in the constructor. After that, changing it is a compile error.

class Order {
  readonly id: number;
  constructor(id: number) { this.id = id; }
}
const o = new Order(1);
// o.id = 2;   // error

readonly vs const: const is for variables; readonly is for properties.

Getters and setters

The idea: get / set accessors let you compute values or validate input while code uses normal property syntax. A getter without a setter is automatically read-only.

class Account {
  private _balance = 0;
  get balance(): number { return this._balance; }
  set balance(v: number) {
    if (v < 0) throw new RangeError('Balance cannot be negative');
    this._balance = v;
  }
}

Inheritance

The idea: extends reuses a parent class. Call super() in the child constructor before using this. Mark overriding methods with override (enable noImplicitOverride to require it), so renaming the parent method later is caught.

class Animal {
  constructor(protected name: string) {}
  speak(): string { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  override speak(): string { return `${this.name} barks`; }
}

Static methods and properties

The idea: static members belong to the class itself. Use them for shared counters, constants and factory methods. They can also be private or readonly.

class IdGen {
  private static next = 1;
  static create(): number { return IdGen.next++; }
}
IdGen.create(); // 1

Abstract classes

The idea: An abstract class is an incomplete base class: it can't be created with new. It can hold shared code, and it lists abstract methods that every subclass must implement.

abstract class Shape {
  abstract area(): number;                 // no body
  describe() { return `Area is ${this.area().toFixed(1)}`; } // shared code
}
class Circle extends Shape {
  constructor(private r: number) { super(); }
  area() { return Math.PI * this.r ** 2; }
}
// new Shape();  // error: cannot create an instance of an abstract class

Practice · 11 questions

Q1private vs #private: what is the difference?Most askedShow answer

TypeScript's private is checked only at compile time; the property is still visible at run time and with as any. JavaScript's #field is enforced by the runtime, truly hidden. # cannot be combined with public/protected.

class A { private x = 1; #y = 2; }
(new A() as any).x;   // 1 - reachable at run time
// (new A() as any).#y // SyntaxError
Q2private vs protected?Show answer

Both hide a member from outside code. protected members can also be used in subclasses; private ones only in the declaring class.

Q3What are parameter properties?Show answer

Adding public, private, protected or readonly before a constructor parameter declares the property and assigns it automatically.

class User {
  constructor(public name: string, private readonly id: number) {}
}
Q4readonly vs const?Show answer

const stops a variable from being reassigned. readonly stops a property from being reassigned after construction. Neither makes nested objects immutable.

Q5What is an abstract class? When would you use one?Show answer

A base class that can't be instantiated, with some shared code and some abstract members that subclasses must implement. Use it when related classes share real implementation and a common contract (e.g. a base Repository with shared save logic and abstract tableName).

Q6What is the override keyword for?Show answer

It marks a method as intentionally replacing a parent method. With noImplicitOverride, forgetting it is an error, and if the parent method is renamed or removed, override makes the compiler warn you.

Q7What does strictPropertyInitialization check? How do you handle late-set fields?Show answer

Every declared property must be set in the constructor or have a default. For fields set later (e.g. by a framework), use the definite assignment ! or make them optional.

class Comp {
  title = '';            // default
  el!: HTMLElement;      // set later, I promise
  data?: string[];       // may be undefined
}
Q8Can a class implement an interface and extend a class at the same time?Show answer
class Car extends Vehicle implements Drivable, Serializable { /* ... */ }

A: Yes: one extends, many implements. implements only checks the shape; it doesn't add any code.

Q9How do you type a class constructor (e.g. for a factory)?Show answer
type Ctor<T> = new (...args: any[]) => T;
function make<T>(C: Ctor<T>): T { return new C(); }
Q10How do getters and setters work in TypeScript? Can they have different types?Show answer

get and set accessors look like a property to callers. A getter with no setter makes the property read-only. Since TypeScript 5.1 the getter and setter types can differ (e.g. accept string | number, return number).

class Temperature {
  private c = 0;
  get celsius(): number { return this.c; }
  set celsius(v: number | string) { this.c = Number(v); }
  get fahrenheit(): number { return this.c * 9 / 5 + 32; } // read-only
}
const t = new Temperature();
t.celsius = '30';
// t.fahrenheit = 100;   // error: read-only
Q11What are static members, and can they use access modifiers?Show answer

static properties and methods belong to the class, not instances. They can be public, private, protected or readonly. A static block (static { }) runs setup code once when the class is defined.

class Config {
  private static instance?: Config;          // singleton pattern
  static readonly VERSION = '1.0';
  private constructor() {}
  static get(): Config {
    return (Config.instance ??= new Config());
  }
}
Config.get() === Config.get();   // true

TypeScript · Section 6

Interfaces

Study notes

Interfaces

The idea: An interface names the shape of an object: which properties and methods it must have. It's a contract. Interfaces disappear at compile time; they only guide the checker. A class can promise to follow one with implements.

interface User {
  readonly id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string;                 // optional
  greet(): string;                // method
  [key: string]: unknown;         // index signature: any other keys allowed
}

interface Comparator { (a: number, b: number): number } // function shape

class Admin implements User {
  constructor(public readonly id: number, public name: string) {}
  greet() { return `Hi, I'm admin ${this.name}`; }
}

Extending interfaces

The idea: interface B extends A copies A's members into B and adds more. An interface can extend several interfaces at once. Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge automatically (declaration merging), which is how libraries let you add fields to their types.

interface Person { name: string }
interface Employee extends Person { salary: number }
interface Manager extends Employee, Auditable { reports: Employee[] }
interface Auditable { createdAt: Date }

// declaration merging
interface Window { appVersion: string }   // adds to the built-in Window type

Interfaces vs abstract classes

Interface Abstract class
Exists at run time No Yes (a real class)
Can contain code No Yes (shared methods)
Constructor / fields with values No Yes
A class can use many Yes (implements A, B) No (extends one)
Access modifiers No (all public) Yes

Rule of thumb: use an interface to describe what something looks like; use an abstract class when subclasses should share how some behaviour works.

Practice · 7 questions

Q1What is an interface? Does it exist at run time?Show answer

A named description of an object's shape. It exists only at compile time; nothing is generated in JavaScript, so you can't use instanceof with an interface.

Q2How do you describe optional, readonly and dynamic keys in an interface?Show answer
interface Config {
  readonly apiUrl: string;
  timeout?: number;
  [header: string]: string | number | undefined; // index signature
}
Q3What is declaration merging?Show answer

Two interface declarations with the same name merge into one. Useful for extending library or global types. type aliases can't merge (a duplicate is an error).

interface Request { user?: { id: number } } // adds 'user' to Express's Request type
Q4How do you extend multiple interfaces? What if they conflict?Show answer

interface C extends A, B {}. If A and B declare the same property with incompatible types, it's an error.

Q5Interface vs abstract class: when to use which?Show answer

Interface: just a contract, no runtime cost, a class can implement many. Abstract class: shares real code and fields, exists at run time, but a class can extend only one.

Q6Can an interface describe a function or a class constructor?Show answer
interface Formatter { (value: number): string }        // call signature
interface ClockCtor { new (h: number): { tick(): void } } // construct signature
const fmt: Formatter = v => v.toFixed(2);
Q7Can an interface extend a class?Show answer

Yes. It takes the class's members (including private/protected ones) as its shape. Then only that class or its subclasses can implement the interface. This is rare in practice.

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 7

Advanced types

Study notes

Intersection types

The idea: A & B is a type that has everything from A and everything from B. Use it to combine small types into a bigger one. (A union A | B is the opposite: either one.)

type HasId = { id: number };
type Timestamps = { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date };
type Product = HasId & Timestamps & { name: string };
const p: Product = { id: 1, name: 'Pen', createdAt: new Date(), updatedAt: new Date() };

Watch out: intersecting conflicting primitives gives never (string & number can't exist).

Type guards

The idea: A type guard is a runtime check that TypeScript understands, so it narrows the type inside the if block. Built-in guards: typeof, instanceof, in, equality, Array.isArray. You can write your own with a return type of value is Type.

interface Fish { swim(): void }
interface Bird { fly(): void }

function isFish(pet: Fish | Bird): pet is Fish {   // custom guard
  return 'swim' in pet;
}
function move(pet: Fish | Bird) {
  if (isFish(pet)) pet.swim();   // pet: Fish
  else pet.fly();                // pet: Bird
}

// assertion function: throws if the check fails
function assertString(v: unknown): asserts v is string {
  if (typeof v !== 'string') throw new TypeError('Expected string');
}

Watch out: TypeScript trusts your custom guard. If its logic is wrong, the types will be wrong too.

Type assertions

The idea: value as Type tells the compiler "treat this as Type, I know better". It does not convert or check anything at run time; it only changes what the compiler believes. Use it sparingly, when you truly know more than the compiler (e.g. DOM elements).

const input = document.querySelector('#email') as HTMLInputElement;
input.value = 'a@b.com';

const cfg = { mode: 'dark' } as const;          // const assertion: readonly literals
// const n = 'hi' as number;                     // error: types too different
const risky = 'hi' as unknown as number;         // double assertion: forced, avoid

Prefer: type guards (real checks) over assertions, and satisfies to check a value against a type without changing its inferred type.

const routes = { home: '/', about: '/about' } satisfies Record<string, string>;
routes.home; // still knows the exact keys

Practice · 8 questions

Q1Union vs intersection: what is the difference?Show answer

A union A | B is a value that is A or B, so you can only use what both share until you narrow. An intersection A & B is a value that is A and B at once, so it has all members of both.

type A = { a: string }; type B = { b: number };
const u: A | B = { a: 'x' };          // either is fine
const i: A & B = { a: 'x', b: 1 };     // needs both
Q2What is a user-defined type guard? Write one.Show answer

A function returning param is Type. When it returns true, TypeScript narrows the argument to that type.

type ApiError = { error: string };
function isApiError(x: unknown): x is ApiError {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'error' in x;
}
Q3What is an assertion function (asserts x is T)?Show answer

A function that throws if a condition fails; after the call, TypeScript treats the value as narrowed for the rest of the scope.

function assertDefined<T>(v: T): asserts v is NonNullable<T> {
  if (v == null) throw new Error('Value is missing');
}
const el = document.getElementById('app');
assertDefined(el);
el.textContent = 'ok';   // el: HTMLElement
Q4Type assertion (as) vs type casting in other languages?Show answer

as changes only the compile-time type; no runtime conversion or check happens. In Java/C#, a cast is checked at run time. A wrong as silently leads to runtime bugs.

Q5When is a type assertion acceptable?Show answer

When you have knowledge the compiler can't have: DOM element types, narrowing after a check the compiler doesn't understand, or test fixtures. Avoid it for API data; validate instead.

Q6What is as const?Show answer

A const assertion: it makes literals keep their exact values, objects/arrays readonly, and arrays become tuples.

const STATUSES = ['active', 'blocked'] as const;
type Status = typeof STATUSES[number]; // 'active' | 'blocked'
Q7What does the satisfies operator do, and how is it different from as or an annotation?Show answer

value satisfies Type checks that the value fits the type, but keeps the value's own more precise inferred type. An annotation replaces the inferred type with the wider one; as skips the check.

type Colors = Record<string, string | number[]>;
const palette = { red: '#f00', green: [0, 255, 0] } satisfies Colors;
palette.green.map(x => x);   // ok: still known as number[]
Q8What is the in operator guard?Show answer
type Car = { drive(): void }; type Boat = { sail(): void };
function go(v: Car | Boat) { 'drive' in v ? v.drive() : v.sail(); }

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 8

Generics

Study notes

Introduction to generics

The idea: Generics are type parameters: placeholders (usually T) filled in when the code is used. They let one function or class work with many types while keeping the link between input and output types. Without generics you'd have to use any and lose type safety.

function firstItem<T>(list: T[]): T | undefined {
  return list[0];
}
const n = firstItem([1, 2, 3]);       // T inferred as number -> n: number | undefined
const s = firstItem<string>(['a']);    // T given explicitly

Picture it: a generic is like a function for types: you pass a type in, you get a fitted type out.

Generic constraints

The idea: T extends Something limits which types are allowed, so you can safely use properties that all those types share. K extends keyof T limits K to the keys of T.

function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;   // .length is safe now
}
longest('apple', 'kiwi');      // ok: strings have length
longest([1, 2], [3]);          // ok: arrays have length
// longest(10, 20);            // error: number has no length

function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}
pluck({ name: 'Asha', age: 25 }, 'age'); // number

Generic classes

The idea: A class with a type parameter; every instance fixes it. Classic examples: a Stack<T>, a typed Repository<T>, a cache.

class Stack<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  push(item: T) { this.items.push(item); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.pop(); }
}
const s = new Stack<number>();
s.push(1);
// s.push('x');   // error

Generic interfaces

The idea: Interfaces (and type aliases) can take type parameters too, with defaults if you like. Very common for API response wrappers.

interface ApiResponse<T, E = string> {
  data: T | null;
  error: E | null;
  status: number;
}
type UserResponse = ApiResponse<{ id: number; name: string }>;

interface Repository<T> {
  getById(id: number): Promise<T>;
  save(item: T): Promise<void>;
}

Built-in generic utility types to know: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, Record<K, V>, ReturnType<F>, Awaited<P>, NonNullable<T>.

Practice · 9 questions

Q1What are generics, and why not just use any?Show answer

Generics are type parameters that make code reusable across types while keeping type safety. any accepts everything but throws away the type, so the result is unchecked. A generic keeps the relationship: what goes in determines what comes out.

function identityAny(x: any) { return x; }   // returns any
function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }  // returns the same type
identity(5).toFixed(2);   // checked
Q2What is a generic constraint? Give an example.Show answer

T extends X restricts T to types assignable to X, so you can use X's members inside.

function getId<T extends { id: number }>(item: T) { return item.id; }
Q3Explain K extends keyof T with an example.Show answer
function setField<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K, value: T[K]) {
  obj[key] = value;
}
const user = { name: 'Asha', age: 25 };
setField(user, 'age', 26);      // ok
// setField(user, 'age', '26'); // error: string not number
// setField(user, 'city', 'x'); // error: no such key
Q4Can generics have default types?Show answer
interface Paginated<T, Meta = { page: number }> { items: T[]; meta: Meta }
const p: Paginated<string> = { items: [], meta: { page: 1 } };
Q5Implement a typed groupBy with generics.Show answer
function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(list: T[], getKey: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> {
  return list.reduce((acc, item) => {
    const k = getKey(item);
    (acc[k] ||= []).push(item);
    return acc;
  }, {} as Record<K, T[]>);
}
groupBy([{ c: 'IN', n: 1 }, { c: 'US', n: 2 }], x => x.c);
Q6Name common built-in generic utility types and what they do.Show answer
Utility Result
Partial<T> all properties optional
Required<T> all properties required
Readonly<T> all properties readonly
Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> only those keys
Omit<T, 'a'> everything except those keys
Record<K, V> object with keys K and values V
Exclude<U, X> / Extract<U, X> remove / keep union members
NonNullable<T> remove null and undefined
ReturnType<F> / Parameters<F> function's return / params
Awaited<P> type inside a promise
Q7When is a generic overkill?Show answer

When the type parameter is used only once (e.g. function log<T>(x: T): void). Then plain unknown is simpler. A good generic links two or more places (input to output, or two parameters).

Q8Write a generic class. Can static members use the class type parameter?Show answer

The type parameter goes after the class name and is fixed per instance. Static members can't use it, because statics belong to the class itself, which is shared by every T.

class TypedCache<K, V> {
  private store = new Map<K, V>();
  set(key: K, value: V) { this.store.set(key, value); return this; }
  get(key: K): V | undefined { return this.store.get(key); }
  // static empty: V;   // error: static members cannot reference class type parameters
}
const prices = new TypedCache<string, number>();
prices.set('pen', 10).set('book', 50);
// prices.set('bag', '20');   // error: string is not number
Q9Generic interface vs generic function type: what is the difference?Show answer
interface Mapper<T, U> { (input: T): U }     // T, U fixed when the interface is used
const toLen: Mapper<string, number> = s => s.length;

interface GenericFn { <T>(x: T): T }         // T chosen at each call
const id: GenericFn = x => x;

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 9

Type operators

Study notes

typeof type operator

The idea: In a type position, typeof someValue gives you the type of an existing variable or function. It lets the code be the single source of truth, so you don't write the same shape twice.

const defaultSettings = { theme: 'light', fontSize: 14, beta: false };
type Settings = typeof defaultSettings;
// { theme: string; fontSize: number; beta: boolean }

function createUser(name: string) { return { name, createdAt: new Date() }; }
type User = ReturnType<typeof createUser>;

Don't confuse: JavaScript's runtime typeof x === 'string' (gives a string at run time) vs TypeScript's type T = typeof x (gives a type at compile time).

keyof operator

The idea: keyof T produces a union of T's property names. Combined with generics, it makes property access type-safe.

type Product = { id: number; name: string; price: number };
type ProductKey = keyof Product;   // 'id' | 'name' | 'price'

function sortBy<T>(list: T[], key: keyof T) {
  return [...list].sort((a, b) => (a[key] > b[key] ? 1 : -1));
}
// sortBy(products, 'cost');   // error: not a key

const labels = { en: 'Hello', te: 'Namaskaram' };
type Lang = keyof typeof labels;   // 'en' | 'te'  (common combo)

Indexed access types

The idea: T['prop'] looks up the type of one property, just like reading a value. Works with unions of keys and with number for array items.

type Order = { id: number; customer: { name: string; city: string }; items: string[] };
type Customer = Order['customer'];          // { name: string; city: string }
type City = Order['customer']['city'];       // string
type Item = Order['items'][number];          // string
type IdOrItems = Order['id' | 'items'];      // number | string[]

Practice · 6 questions

Q1What is the difference between JavaScript typeof and TypeScript's typeof type operator?Show answer

In an expression, typeof x runs at run time and returns a string like 'number'. In a type position (type T = typeof x), it is a compile-time operator that copies the full static type of x.

Q2How do you get a union of an object's keys? Of its values?Show answer
const ROLES = { admin: 'ADMIN', editor: 'EDITOR' } as const;
type RoleKey = keyof typeof ROLES;              // 'admin' | 'editor'
type RoleValue = typeof ROLES[keyof typeof ROLES]; // 'ADMIN' | 'EDITOR'
Q3What does keyof return for a type with an index signature?Show answer

For { [k: string]: number }, keyof gives string | number (number keys are converted to strings in JavaScript). For { [k: number]: X } it gives number.

Q4Write a type-safe get(obj, key) function.Show answer
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}
const cfg = { port: 3000, host: 'localhost' };
const port = get(cfg, 'port');   // number
Q5How do you get the type of an array's items or a nested property?Show answer
const users = [{ id: 1, tags: ['a'] }];
type User = typeof users[number];       // { id: number; tags: string[] }
type Tag = User['tags'][number];          // string
Q6Can indexed access use a variable?Show answer

No. The index must be a type, not a runtime value: write T['name'] or T[typeof key], not T[key] where key is a variable.

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 10

Mapped and conditional types

Study notes

Mapped types

The idea: A mapped type builds a new object type by looping over keys: { [K in Keys]: NewType }. Think of it as map() for types. Modifiers let you add or remove readonly and ? (-readonly, -?), and as lets you rename keys.

type User = { name: string; age: number };

type Optional<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };          // like Partial
type Frozen<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };     // like Readonly
type Flags<T> = { [K in keyof T]: boolean };            // same keys, boolean values
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
// Getters<User> = { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }

Most built-in utilities (Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Record) are mapped types.

Conditional types

The idea: T extends U ? X : Y picks one type or another based on whether T fits U. It's an if for types. With a union, it runs on each member separately (distributive). infer lets you capture a piece of a type inside the condition.

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? 'yes' : 'no';
type A = IsString<'hi'>;           // 'yes'

type NoNull<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;
type B = NoNull<string | null>;     // string  (distributes over the union)

type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : T;
type C = ElementOf<number[]>;       // number

type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
type D = Unwrap<Promise<string>>;   // string

Built-ins made this way: Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited.

Practice · 8 questions

Q1What is a mapped type? Implement Partial and Readonly yourself.Show answer
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type MyReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type MyRequired<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };   // -? removes optional
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }; // removes readonly
Q2Implement Pick and Record.Show answer
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type MyRecord<K extends PropertyKey, V> = { [P in K]: V };
Q3How do you rename or filter keys in a mapped type?Show answer

Use as in the key part. Mapping a key to never removes it.

type OnlyStrings<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
type Prefixed<T> = { [K in keyof T as `api_${string & K}`]: T[K] };
Q4What is a conditional type? What does "distributive" mean?Show answer

T extends U ? X : Y chooses a type based on assignability. When T is a bare type parameter and receives a union, the condition is applied to each member separately and the results are joined. Wrap in brackets ([T] extends [U]) to stop this.

type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type A = ToArray<string | number>;   // string[] | number[]  (distributed)
type ToArray2<T> = [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never;
type B = ToArray2<string | number>;  // (string | number)[]
Q5What does infer do? Implement ReturnType.Show answer

infer X declares a type variable to be captured from the matched pattern.

type MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type MyParameters<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;
Q6Implement Exclude, Extract and NonNullable.Show answer
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type MyExtract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never;
type MyNonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;
Q7Write a DeepReadonly type.Most askedShow answer
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => any
  ? T
  : T extends object
    ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
    : T;
Q8What are template literal types?Show answer

String types built from other types with backtick syntax. They work with unions to generate all combinations.

type Size = 'sm' | 'lg'; type Color = 'red' | 'blue';
type ClassName = `${Size}-${Color}`;  // 'sm-red' | 'sm-blue' | 'lg-red' | 'lg-blue'
type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`; // 'click' -> 'onClick'

↑ Back to contents

TypeScript · Section 11

Modules

Study notes

Modules

The idea: TypeScript uses the same ES module syntax as JavaScript (import / export), and you can also export and import types. Any file with a top-level import or export is a module with its own scope; a file without one is a global script (its declarations leak everywhere).

// models.ts
export interface User { id: number; name: string }
export type Role = 'admin' | 'user';
export function makeUser(name: string): User { return { id: Date.now(), name }; }
export default class UserService {}

// app.ts
import UserService, { makeUser, type User } from './models';
import type { Role } from './models';   // type-only: removed from output

Remember:

  • import type / export type bring in types only; they are fully erased, which avoids loading code you don't need at run time.
  • The module and moduleResolution settings decide how imports are written in the output and how paths are found (node16/nodenext for Node, bundler for Vite/webpack).
  • Under Node ESM, relative imports need the .js extension even in .ts files (import x from './util.js').
  • .d.ts files hold only type declarations, for libraries written in JavaScript. Install them with npm i -D @types/library.
  • paths in tsconfig sets short import aliases (@/utils); the bundler must be told about them too.

Practice · 6 questions

Q1What makes a TypeScript file a module instead of a script?Show answer

Having at least one top-level import or export. Without one, its declarations are global and can clash with other files. Add export {} to force module scope.

Q2What is import type, and why use it?Show answer

It imports only types, which are always erased from the output. This avoids accidentally loading a module (and its side effects) at run time, and is required with verbatimModuleSyntax/isolatedModules when importing types.

import type { User } from './models';
import { type Role, createUser } from './models'; // inline form
Q3What is a .d.ts file?Show answer

A declaration file that contains only types (no code). It describes the shape of a JavaScript library so TypeScript can check your use of it. Found in the library itself or in @types/* packages, or written by you.

// legacy-lib.d.ts
declare module 'legacy-lib' {
  export function slugify(text: string): string;
}
Q4How do you add a property to a global or third-party type?Show answer

Use declaration merging inside declare global or declare module.

declare global {
  interface Window { analytics: { track(e: string): void } }
}
export {};
Q5module vs moduleResolution in tsconfig?Show answer

module controls the import/export syntax written to output (ESNext, NodeNext, CommonJS). moduleResolution controls how import paths are found (nodenext follows Node's rules, bundler follows Vite/webpack rules).

Q6What are namespaces? Should you use them?Show answer

namespace X { ... } is an older TypeScript way to group code under one name. Modern code uses ES modules instead; namespaces still appear in some .d.ts files.

TypeScript · Section 12

Tooling (Node.js, Vite)

Study notes

Node.js with TypeScript

The idea: Add TypeScript and Node's type definitions, configure tsconfig.json, then either compile to JavaScript and run that, or use a runner for development.

npm init -y
npm install -D typescript @types/node tsx
npx tsc --init

Suggested tsconfig.json basics for a Node project: "target": "ES2022", "module": "nodenext", "moduleResolution": "nodenext", "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src", "strict": true.

// package.json scripts
{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "tsx watch src/index.ts",
    "build": "tsc",
    "start": "node dist/index.js"
  }
}

Note: recent Node versions can run simple .ts files directly by stripping types, but they don't type-check, so you still run tsc for checking.

Vite with TypeScript

The idea: Vite is a fast build tool for front-end apps. It strips TypeScript types instantly using esbuild, but it does not type-check. The template adds a tsc step to the build for that.

npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template vanilla-ts   # or react-ts, vue-ts
cd my-app && npm install
npm run dev      # dev server with instant reload
npm run build    # tsc (type-check) + vite build -> dist/

Remember: in Vite projects tsconfig usually has "noEmit": true and "moduleResolution": "bundler", because Vite creates the output, not tsc. Environment variables are typed through import.meta.env and a vite-env.d.ts file.

Practice · 6 questions

Q1How do you set up TypeScript for a Node.js project?Show answer

Install typescript, @types/node and a dev runner (tsx), run tsc --init, set module/moduleResolution to nodenext, outDir: dist, strict: true. Use tsx watch in development and tsc then node dist/index.js for production.

Q2Why do Vite and esbuild projects still run tsc?Show answer

Vite/esbuild only strip types to be fast; they never report type errors. Running tsc --noEmit (in the build script or CI) is what actually checks types.

Q3What is isolatedModules, and why do bundlers need it?Show answer

Tools like esbuild and Babel compile one file at a time without seeing the whole project. isolatedModules makes TypeScript warn about features that need cross-file information (like re-exporting a type without export type, or const enum across files).

Q4What are @types packages?Show answer

Community-maintained type declarations (from DefinitelyTyped) for JavaScript libraries that don't ship their own. Install as dev dependencies: npm i -D @types/express.

Q5How do you speed up type-checking in a big project?Show answer

Use incremental: true (caches results), project references (composite + references) to split the codebase, skipLibCheck: true to skip checking .d.ts files in node_modules, and avoid very deep generic types.

Q6How do you debug TypeScript in VS Code?Show answer

Enable sourceMap: true so the debugger maps compiled JavaScript back to your .ts lines, then set breakpoints directly in the .ts files (or debug through tsx).
